issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This probe compared upstream-shaped FlashAttention-4 THD/varlen attention against Marin's current Grug segmented FA4/CuTe path on B200 for the exact d5120 Grug causal attention shape. The measured THD compact `cu_seqlens` path was materially faster than the current segmented FA4/CuTe implementation across the tested packed layouts, but the usable prototype is still a torch/DLPack bridge rather than a JIT-safe JAX FFI. The recommended integration direction is fixed max-segment metadata plus a real THD/JAX FFI path, while avoiding the private JAX cuDNN packed-offset path until its exact-GQA numerics are validated.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6059
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Issue5815 needs a narrow benchmark of upstream-shaped FlashAttention-4 THD/varlen attention against the current Grug dense BSHD segmented FA4/CuTe port on B200. The target shape is the exact d5120 Grug causal self-attention q/k/v layout: q `[B,S,Hq,D]`, k/v `[B,S,Hkv,D]`.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Determine whether reshaping BSHD to THD, building `cu_seqlens` from packed segment IDs or fixed segment metadata, and calling upstream FA4 CuTe varlen materially beats the current segmented FA4 path for fwd+bwd. Thresholds: `<=0.005s` promising, `0.005-0.010s` marginal, `>0.010s` not worth pursuing for issue5815.

### Links

* Stable research tag: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529
* Stable research logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md
* Stable probe script: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/issue5815-fa4-thd-logbook-20260529/scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py
* Draft PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6059
* Code paths: `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py`, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_thd.py`

## Results

Latest focused B200 probe for exact d5120, `S=4096,Hq=40,Hkv=8,D=128`, dynamic uneven segments:

| segs/row | B | dense upstream | current FA4/CuTe | THD fixed lengths | THD compact cu-lens |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | 0.000681s | 0.001939s | 0.000892s | 0.000656s |
| 2 | 4 | 0.002399s | 0.006653s | 0.002391s | 0.002151s |
| 4 | 1 | 0.000680s | 0.001280s | 0.000790s | 0.000561s |
| 4 | 4 | 0.002343s | 0.004249s | 0.002028s | 0.001801s |

## Decision log

* 2026-05-29: The public upstream PyTorch varlen wrapper alone was not enough; internal upstream FA4 `_flash_attn_fwd/_flash_attn_bwd` is the relevant API for the THD/cu-lens core.
* 2026-05-29: Fixed max-segment metadata is a useful integration point. It is materially faster than current segmented FA4/CuTe and avoids scanning full `[B,S]` segment IDs in the attention hot path.
* 2026-05-29: Do not use the private JAX cuDNN packed-offset path for exact Grug GQA until its GQA numerics are validated.

## Negative results index

* Public `flash_attn_varlen_func` autograd was slower than the internal upstream fwd/bwd API.
* Private JAX cuDNN packed offsets were fast but failed numerics for exact `Hq=40,Hkv=8` GQA.
* Including full dynamic `segment_ids -> cu_seqlens` construction inside the timed helper can erase the THD kernel win on small cases.

## Current baseline

Shape `B in {1,4} S=4096 Hq=40 Hkv=8 D=128`, bf16, causal fwd+bwd, dynamic uneven contiguous segments. Latest focused medians are listed in Results.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS.md and skills
- [x] Fetch issue and related context (#5815, #5896)
- [x] Inspect current FA4/CuTe code paths in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/`
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (open PRs/issues)
- [x] Post Research + Proposed Approach (this comment)
- [ ] Implementation deferred — needs human go-ahead (research scope + B200 hardware)

# Research

This is a research experiment, not a self-contained bug fix. To produce the probe results the issue asks for, three things are needed and none exist on `main` today: (1) the probe script `scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py` (the `scratch/` tree is empty here); (2) the `fa4_thd_core` THD/varlen entry — `gpu_fa4_cute_attention` only takes BSHD with packed `segment_ids` and routes to the segmented (non-cu_seqlens) backward, which explicitly disables varlen paths; (3) a `jax_cudnn_core` reference path (no such symbol in tree). Plus B200 access to actually run it. This exceeds the 100-LOC self-contained bug-fix threshold, so deferring to human review before implementation.

**Relevant code**
- [`_fa4_cute.py#L130-L159`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L130-L159) — current BSHD entry; consumes `AttentionMask.segment_ids`, computes per-token causal lower bounds, calls `fa4_cute_attention_forward`
- [`_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py#L44`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py#L44) — "upstream varlen/THD cu_seqlens paths are intentionally disabled"
- [`_fa4_cute_kernels.py#L54-L58`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute_kernels.py#L54-L58) — segmented kernel uses per-token bounds, not cu_seqlens
- [`_core.py#L21-L25`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py#L21-L25) — `GrugAttentionImplementation` literal lists only `reference`, `tpu_splash`, `gpu_fa4_cute`; no cuDNN or THD variant registered
- #5896 logbook — B200 FA4/CuTe baseline `(B=1,S=8192,Hq=32,Hkv=8,D=128,seg=256)` BF16: patched FA4 fwd+bwd `1.021 ms`, TE flash `1.229 ms`

# Proposed Approach

Design change — write before coding because the THD path does not exist.

Step 1: Add `fa4_thd_core` entry. New function in `_fa4_cute.py` that takes BSHD `q/k/v` plus `segment_ids`, reshapes BSHD → THD (`q: [B*S, Hq, D]`), and either (a) calls upstream `flash_attn.cute` varlen forward/backward directly with `cu_seqlens_q = jnp.arange(B+1, dtype=jnp.int32) * S` and `max_seqlen_q = S` — single-sequence-per-row, so the layout matches what the issue specifies — or (b) wires a thin JAX FFI wrapper around the CuTe varlen entry. Option (a) is preferred for the probe; (b) only if upstream lacks a JAX-callable handle.

Step 2: Add `jax_cudnn_core` reference. Wrap `jax.nn.dot_product_attention(..., implementation="cudnn")` with the same BSHD-in / BSHD-out signature so the three paths are directly comparable. jax cuDNN does not natively take packed segment_ids; for the probe use `is_causal=True` on the single-sequence-per-batch-row layout the issue defines.

Step 3: Write `scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py`. Driver that builds the d5120 Grug shape (issue does not pin `B/S/Hq/Hkv/D` — confirm with #5815; #5896 used `B=1, S=8192, Hq=32, Hkv=8, D=128`), runs each of `jax_cudnn_core`, `fa4_cute_core`, `fa4_thd_core` for fwd and fwd+bwd with a fixed `warmup=3, steps=10` loop, and prints steady-state ms plus value/grad max-abs vs a small-seq reference. Match the format used in the #5896 logbook so the result is appendable.

Step 4: Run on B200 (Slurm), apply the decision rule from the issue (`<=0.005s` promising / `0.005-0.010s` marginal / `>0.010s` skip) to fwd+bwd steady, and post the structured result back here.

Open questions to confirm before implementation:
- Target shape: take #5896 `(B=1,S=8192,Hq=32,Hkv=8,D=128)` or a different d5120 spec from #5815?
- Should `fa4_thd_core` call upstream `flash_attn.cute` varlen directly, or land a JAX FFI wrapper in `_fa4_cute_backend.py`?
- Who has B200 capacity to run this — should I prepare the probe script as a PR and hand off, or wait?

Estimated change size: ~150-300 LOC (probe + thd entry + cudnn entry + minimal test). Above the 100-LOC threshold, so awaiting confirmation before opening a PR.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: FA4 THD/varlen probe complete

- Change: Added an experimental THD path that reshapes BSHD to `[B*S,H,D]`, derives `cu_seqlens` from contiguous packed segment ID starts, and calls `flash_attn.cute.flash_attn_varlen_func` from `flash-attn-4==4.0.0b15`.
- Result delta: For `B=1 S=4096 Hq=40 Hkv=8 D=128`, dynamic `segment_len=1024` medians were cuDNN `0.000753s`, current segmented FA4/CuTe `0.001085s`, upstream THD `0.001570s`. Full-sequence `segment_len=4096` medians were cuDNN `0.000752s`, current segmented FA4/CuTe `0.003082s`, upstream THD `0.001869s`.
- Confidence: exploratory, single focused B200 run with 10 timed iterations after warmup.
- Links: `.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md`, `scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py`.
- Next: Treat THD as promising in absolute terms but not a clear issue5815 fix for dynamic multi-segment packed rows; cuDNN remains fastest.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: B and segment-count sweep with cuDNN segment packing

- Change: Re-ran the probe with `B={1,2,4}` and `segment_len={4096,2048,1024}`. The cuDNN row now packs each contiguous segment into its own batch row before causal attention, so it matches multi-segment packed semantics instead of treating the full row as one sequence.
- Result delta: cuDNN-with-packing was fastest in every case. For `segment_len=1024`: `B=1` cuDNN `0.000441s`, FA4/CuTe `0.001091s`, THD `0.001588s`; `B=2` cuDNN `0.000694s`, FA4/CuTe `0.001913s`, THD `0.002271s`; `B=4` cuDNN `0.001191s`, FA4/CuTe `0.003562s`, THD `0.003648s`.
- Confidence: exploratory but stronger than the first pass; this covers one, two, and four contiguous segments per row across local batch sizes 1, 2, and 4.
- Links: `.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md`, `scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py`.
- Next: For issue5815, prioritize a packed-cuDNN implementation path over upstream THD if the production packed rows can be represented as contiguous segment ranges.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: dynamic unequal segment-length THD probe

- Change: Updated the probe to generate unequal contiguous segment lengths per row. The FA4 THD row uses compact THD `[total_tokens,H,D]` plus cumulative sequence lengths from segment starts. The cuDNN row uses padded segment rows plus sequence lengths because JAX cuDNN does not expose the same THD cumulative-length API.
- Result delta: For two uneven segments per row (`~[1365,2731]`), padded cuDNN errored on unsupported sequence length `2731`; THD beat current FA4/CuTe: `B=1` `0.001684s` vs `0.001970s`, `B=2` `0.002508s` vs `0.003547s`, `B=4` `0.004144s` vs `0.006702s`. For four uneven segments per row (`~[409,819,1228,1640]`), THD was slower at `B=1` but slightly faster by `B=2`/`B=4`: `B=4` THD `0.003757s` vs FA4/CuTe `0.004313s`.
- Confidence: exploratory; covers unequal contiguous segment lengths but not padded `-1` holes or non-contiguous repeated IDs.
- Links: `.agents/logbooks/issue5815-fa4-thd.md`, `scratch/issue5815_attention_backend_probe.py`.
- Next: Treat upstream THD/cu-seqlens as the dynamic packed candidate. Do not treat padded cuDNN as an equivalent replacement for arbitrary dynamic segment lengths.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Update: there is a lower-level JAX cuDNN packed-offset path that is not exposed through public `jax.nn.dot_product_attention`.

API used in the scratch probe:

`jax._src.cudnn.fused_attention_stablehlo.dot_product_attention(q, k, v, q_seqlen=..., kv_seqlen=..., q_offsets=..., kv_offsets=..., scale=1/sqrt(D), mask_type=MaskType.CAUSAL, qkv_layout="BTNH")`

For dynamic unequal contiguous segments, I pass inputs as `[B,S,H,D]`, `q_offsets/kv_offsets` as `[B,max_segments+1]`, and `q_seqlen/kv_seqlen` as `[B,max_segments]` with per-row segment lengths. This is closer to the packed/offset path we wanted than the public padded `jax.nn` sequence-length baseline.

B200 fwd+bwd medians for exact `S=4096 Hq=40 Hkv=8 D=128` dynamic Grug shape, one shape per Python process:

| segments per row | B | jax_cudnn_offsets_core |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | 0.000708s |
| 2 | 2 | 0.001088s |
| 2 | 4 | 0.001878s |
| 4 | 1 | 0.000576s |
| 4 | 2 | 0.000880s |
| 4 | 4 | 0.001492s |

For comparison, the prior dynamic sweep had upstream FA4 THD at `0.001684/0.002508/0.004144s` for 2 segments at B=1/2/4 and `0.001591/0.002325/0.003757s` for 4 segments at B=1/2/4. Current local FA4/CuTe was slower than THD in the dynamic 2-segment case and roughly tied/lower only in the small 4-segment B=1 case.

Caveat: this is private `jax._src` API, not a stable public JAX surface. The offset path also showed process-level fragility when sweeping multiple offset shapes in one Python process: isolated one-shape processes completed, while a same-process shape sweep hit a CUDA illegal-address after a shape transition. That needs numerics and stability validation before any production use.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Correction on the private cuDNN offsets result: the fast `jax_cudnn_offsets_core` timings are not valid evidence for the exact Grug GQA shape yet.

I added a numerics check against `reference_attention` using the private offsets API with `MaskType.PADDING_CAUSAL` and start-offset encoding from the JAX docstring.

Results on a small dynamic segmented case, `S=1024 segments_per_row=4`:

| shape | output max abs | output mean abs | status |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `Hq=40 Hkv=8` | 4.843750 | 0.166690 | invalid |
| `Hq=8 Hkv=8` | 0.015625 | 0.000476 | expected bf16 range |

The MHA control passing while the exact GQA shape fails points to a GQA + packed-offset limitation/bug in this private JAX/cuDNN path, not a simple segment-offset construction issue. So: yes, the private cuDNN path exists and is very fast, but I would not use it for issue5815 unless we can get/fix a validated GQA packed-offset API.

For now, upstream FA4 THD remains the valid dynamic-packed candidate from this probe; private cuDNN offsets are an interesting follow-up, not a drop-in replacement for the d5120 Grug shape.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 B200 FA4 tile tuning update.

I verified the dense/no-segment upstream path separately from the Grug segmented port. Using `flash-attn-4==4.0.0b15` internal dense FA4 calls on `S=4096 Hq=40 Hkv=8 D=128`:

| config | B=1 | B=4 |
|---|---:|---:|
| upstream default | 0.000677s | 0.002316s |
| explicit `128x128` fwd + `128x128` bwd | 0.000677s | 0.002423s |
| `128x64` fwd + `128x128` bwd | 0.000706s | 0.002696s |
| `128x64` fwd + `64x64` bwd | 0.000707s | 0.002620s |
| `128x128` fwd + `64x64` bwd | 0.000677s | 0.002496s |

So yes: when there are no segment IDs, upstream's default block choice is the fastest or tied-fastest for this shape.

For the Grug segmented JAX/CuTe port, that dense upstream block size does not transfer: explicit `128x128` made the segmented path much slower because our port is not the native upstream SM100 dense kernel; it carries dynamic lower-bound metadata through the segmented fork. The best tested B200 config was `64x64` forward and `64x64` backward, 128 threads.

Segmented FA4/CuTe before -> after `64x64` override:

| dynamic layout | B | old | new |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 segments/row | 1 | 0.001984s | 0.001936s |
| 2 segments/row | 4 | 0.006709s | 0.006639s |
| 4 segments/row | 1 | 0.001321s | 0.001281s |
| 4 segments/row | 4 | 0.004309s | 0.004253s |

Final post-change comparison against upstream THD:

| dynamic layout | B | FA4/CuTe segmented | upstream THD |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 segments/row | 1 | 0.001941s | 0.001722s |
| 2 segments/row | 4 | 0.006664s | 0.004183s |
| 4 segments/row | 1 | 0.001289s | 0.001604s |
| 4 segments/row | 4 | 0.004252s | 0.003797s |

Conclusion: the B200 segmented FA4 config tweak is a small consistent win, but it does not change the larger issue5815 conclusion: THD remains better for two uneven segments and larger B/four segments, while segmented FA4/CuTe still wins the B=1/four-short-segment case.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up on fixed max-segment metadata:

Implemented and probed a middle path between raw `segment_ids` and fully precomputed compact `cu_seqlens`:

- `GrugLmExample.causal(..., max_segments=...)` can now eagerly build fixed-shape THD segment metadata.
- The metadata is `(segment_lengths, num_segments)`, padded to `max_segments`; packed datasets pass `max_segments_per_example + 1` so a trailing padding run has room.
- `gpu_fa4_thd` prefers this metadata when present and compacts the small `[B, max_segments]` length table to upstream FA4 `cu_seqlens` at the backend boundary.
- The scratch probe now has `fa4_thd_lengths_core` for this exact path.

Focused B200 probe, exact d5120 shape `S=4096,Hq=40,Hkv=8,D=128`, dynamic uneven segments:

| segs/row | B | dense upstream | current FA4/CuTe | THD fixed lengths | THD compact cu-lens |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | 0.000681s | 0.001939s | 0.000892s | 0.000656s |
| 2 | 4 | 0.002399s | 0.006653s | 0.002391s | 0.002151s |
| 4 | 1 | 0.000680s | 0.001280s | 0.000790s | 0.000561s |
| 4 | 4 | 0.002343s | 0.004249s | 0.002028s | 0.001801s |

Validation: local `py_compile` passed for the edited modules and probe; the focused B200 probe completed successfully. cuDNN segmented did not produce a usable baseline for these dynamic uneven rows: two segments rejected the max sequence length, and four segments hit a cuDNN execution-plan finalize error.

Interpretation: fixed max-segment metadata is materially faster than the current Grug segmented FA4/CuTe port and is comfortably under the issue threshold. It still leaves ~0.2us overhead versus fully precomputed compact `cu_seqlens`, most visible at B=1, because the backend still compacts fixed lengths to FA4's compact API inside the timed path.

issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tested whether routed expert MuonH parameters in the May Grug MoE recipe should use a different learning-rate scale because each expert only sees a sparse subset of tokens. Gate 1 compared three normalizations: shrinking only routed expert LR by sqrt(sparsity), boosting the dense/non-expert MuonH LR, and a mid-ratio compromise. `boost-nonexpert` and `shrink-expert` both failed gate 1, while `mid-ratio` passed with modest effective speedups at d512 and d768, so gate 2 was launched for d1024 and d1280. The larger gate-2 run was still in recovery/monitoring in the latest issue updates, with most follow-up work focused on TPU preemptions, regional checkpoint restore, host RAM, and launcher fixes rather than a final gate-2 decision.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4474840407
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4477551329
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5799#issuecomment-4480453273
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## TL;DR

Test whether routed expert MuonH weights should use a smaller LR because each expert sees only a sparse fraction of tokens. Gate 1 compares two normalizations at d512 and d768 against the MoE effective-speedup gates.

## Original prompt

> I want to test the following idea on the per-expert learning rate, the per expert learning rate should be smaller as each expert see less token. My guess is that we should shrink the per-expert learning rate down by \sqrt{sparsity} (assuming sparsity is between [0,1]). On top of this idea, there are two potential candidate: we can either keep the learning rate on the remaining muonh parameters the same and decrease the per-expert learning rate; or keep the per-expert learning rate the same and increase the remaining learning rate. Let's try to do gate 1 for both and potentially do gate 2 if either pass gate1.

## Scope

Builds on #5763 (`may_arch + GN->MuonH + 1% warmup + no grad-clip`) and keeps that recipe fixed except for the MuonH LR split.

For may_arch, `num_experts_per_token=4` and `num_experts=256`, so `sparsity = 4 / 256 = 1/64` and `sqrt(sparsity) = 0.125`.

Gate-1 candidates:

| candidate | routed expert MuonH LR | remaining MuonH LR | Adam/AdamH groups |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| shrink-expert | 0.125x heuristic | 1.0x heuristic | unchanged |
| boost-nonexpert | 1.0x heuristic | 8.0x heuristic | unchanged |

Only routed expert MLP weights are in the `muonh_expert` bucket. Shared expert weights, attention matrices, and GatedNorm weights stay in the remaining MuonH bucket because they see dense traffic.

## Gate plan

Gate 1:
- d512 at 2.19e17 FLOPs
- d768 at 1.70e18 FLOPs

If either candidate shows effective speedup at both scales, run gate 2 for that candidate at:
- d1024 at 9.00e18 FLOPs
- d1280 at 2.83e19 FLOPs

## Links

- Branch: `moe_muonh_may_arch_per_expert_lr_gate1`
- Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe/muonh_may_arch_per_expert_lr_gate1.py`
- Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/moe_per_expert_lr_sqrt_sparsity.md`

## Decision log

| Date | Decision | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-05-17 | Start with gate 1 only for both normalizations. | This isolates the LR normalization question before spending d1024/d1280 compute. |

## Negative results index

None yet.

## Current baseline

Use `experiments/grug/moe/README.md` compute-optimal baseline and `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md` effective-speedup gate definitions.

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
The inference dashboard does not report request-level TPOT. It queries `time_per_output_token_seconds_{bucket,count,sum}`, while pinned GPU and TPU vLLM versions and live Marin telemetry expose `request_time_per_output_token_seconds_{bucket,count,sum}`. The existing `tpot` rows instead contain inter-token latency, which is a different distribution.

Reproduce:
1. Open the inference dashboard for a serve that emits both latency families.
2. Inspect the latency rows.

Expected: report request-level TPOT and inter-token latency as separate latency families.

<details>
<summary>Supporting evidence</summary>

- [The dashboard maps both source names to `tpot`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ebba6d565b4e9dfd3e11b60cf22e8936737f804e/infra/grafana/src/vllm_observability.py#L68-L74), but the unprefixed request family is not emitted by the pinned vLLM versions.
- Live `telemetry_v1` data contains the request-prefixed histogram components and no unprefixed counterparts.
- [The latency fixture covers only inter-token latency](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/ebba6d565b4e9dfd3e11b60cf22e8936737f804e/infra/grafana/tests/test_vllm_observability.py#L208-L212).
- Request TPOT contributes one mean decode time per completed request. Inter-token latency measures gaps between emitted tokens.

</details>
issues.title: [grafana] Inference dashboard misses request-level TPOT

issues.author: yonromai
issues.body:
The production inference dashboard cannot load views backed by `/v1/vllm/overview`. The generated overview SQL repeats unaliased expressions inside `UNION ALL` projections, so Finelog rejects the query during planning and the endpoint returns HTTP 500.

Expected behavior: the overview endpoint should return data for a valid vLLM serve, and its dashboard panels should render.

<details>
<summary>Supporting evidence</summary>

- The failure occurs on deployed Grafana revision `marin-grafana-00105-bp5`.
- The selected serve contains both `request_time_per_output_token_seconds_*` and `inter_token_latency_seconds_*` samples.
- The actual Grafana datasource request for the latency panel returns a downstream HTTP 500.
- Cloud Run reports:

  ```text
  Error during planning: Projections require unique expression names but the expression "CAST(NULL AS Int64)" at position 0 and "CAST(NULL AS Utf8)" at position 7 have the same name. Consider aliasing ("AS") one of them.
  ```

- A minimal Finelog query containing unaliased null casts reproduces the failure; naming those projections succeeds.
- This was found while smoke-testing #8573. The offending output projections predate that PR, which changed only the latency-family mappings.

</details>
issues.title: [grafana] vLLM overview SQL has duplicate projection names

The weekly fork-migration system from #8048 is in place: a refresh-fork skill and
per-fork descriptors (#8068, #8117), a weekly ferry coordinator (#8245) with Loom
federation (#8284), and automated re-pinning for the vLLM GPU wheel (#8292). The TPU
vLLM stack refreshed to tpu-inference v0.26.0 (#8207) on top of the externalized
stack (#8063), and the GPU wheel now discovers its `_C` extension by shape across the
CUDA 13 / stable-ABI boundary (#8250). This issue tracks the work that remains after
that rollout, and is the canonical fork-migration tracker going forward. It supersedes
#8048 and folds in the refresh trackers #8298, #7097, #7143, and #6480.

1. Promote the Harbor one-time catch-up. marin-community/harbor#73 re-ports the fork
   overlay onto current upstream and folds the standalone `harbor-config` package into
   `harbor.models`. It is mergeable with `marin-precommit`, `marin-style-sync`, and
   `tests` green. Two steps need an admin/reviewer: drop the retired `harbor-config`
   context from the fork `main` branch protection (it no longer reports, so it blocks
   the merge), then review and merge, and promote the caught-up tree to protected
   `main`. Done when fork `main` carries the caught-up overlay and its protection no
   longer requires `harbor-config`.

2. Bump the Marin Harbor pin. After harbor#73 lands, re-pin `config/external/harbor`

   keep the migration.toml [harbor] nuances. The aime-smoke e2e already passed

   `harbor[analysis,datasets,daytona]` floating on `main` plus the standalone
   `harbor-config` wheel, so the harbor.models fold in harbor#73 breaks any SkyRL

   `harbor.models`, and give SkyRL a Marin-style update-external plus one terminal-bench
   e2e. Cadence stays decoupled and coordinated on breaking changes rather than weekly

   no blocker for evalchemy. Confirm whether that is a legitimate no-op (the fork
   already matches upstream `main`) or a silent failure, and have the leg emit an
   explicit no-op summary either way.

5. Publish prebuilt TPU vLLM fork wheels (#7143). Cold TPU jobs still source-build the
   `vllm` and `tpu-inference` forks; a Marin-controlled index would let serve, eval,
   and RL install a pinned wheel. Standalone spec in #7143.

6. Resolve the Marin-owned pin audit (#6480). Decide whether Levanter can move to a
   Transformers 5 range and drop the tpu-inference Gemma4 guard, and keep the
   JAX/libtpu/torch/torchvision alignment documented against the fork stack. The

issues.author: claude[bot]
issues.body:
The Tier-1 datakit smoke ferry failed. The `datakit-smoke/verify_fuzzy_dups` step raised, propagated through `StepRunner` (`RuntimeError: 1 step(s) failed`), and failed the ferry job. The driver runs with `max_task_failures=0`, so a single step failure fails the canary.

Root cause: `verify_fuzzy_dups` loads a distributed in-memory document store. A verify worker was preempted and restarted mid-run (worker 66 reached `attempt=1` and reinstalled its venv at 08:50) on the preemptible v4 pool. When the memory-store load poll re-resolved to the restarted actor, that actor no longer held the in-flight operation, so Iris returned `ConnectError: Operation '94446ed7…' not found` (`Code.NOT_FOUND`). `is_retryable_error` classifies `NOT_FOUND` as a non-retryable application error (`lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/errors.py:135`), and `actor_result_with_recovery` only recovers `TimeoutError` and `ActorUnavailableError` (`lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/memory_store.py:301-314`). The `NOT_FOUND` therefore propagates and fails the step.

Reproduce:
1. Run `experiments.ferries.datakit_ferry` on preemptible TPU workers.
2. Preempt or restart a verify worker while `verify_fuzzy_dups` is in its memory-store load pass.
3. The load poll re-resolves to the restarted actor, which returns `NOT_FOUND` for the in-flight operation, and the step fails.

Expected: A memory-store actor restart during the load pass should re-issue the load against the recovered actor, the way `ActorUnavailableError` already triggers re-issue in `actor_result_with_recovery`. An operation lost to an actor restart is recoverable, not fatal.

<details>
<summary>Trimmed traceback (driver task 0)</summary>

```
File "lib/marin/src/marin/processing/classification/deduplication/verify_fuzzy_dups.py", line 835, in verify_fuzzy_dups
    document_store = ctx.load_memory_store(...)
File "lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py", line 407, in load_pass
    actor_result_with_recovery(...)
File "lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/memory_store.py", line 300, in actor_result_with_recovery
    return future.result(timeout=max(0.0, remaining))
File "lib/fray/src/fray/iris_backend.py", line 413, in result
    op = self._client.poll_operation_status(self._op_id)
File "lib/iris/src/iris/actor/client.py", line 183, in poll_operation_status
File "lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/actor_connect.py", line 482, in get_operation
connectrpc.errors.ConnectError: Operation '94446ed71a9743a997e75ec1a9966e23' not found

RuntimeError: Step failed: datakit-smoke/verify_fuzzy_dups_8a99f4b7
RuntimeError: 1 step(s) failed
```
</details>

Evidence:
- `iris job describe /runner/iris-run-job-20260824-073906`: `State: failed`, `failures=1`, `Error: RuntimeError: 1 step(s) failed`; task 0 ran 1h16m.
- Verify worker 66 reached `attempt=1` and reinstalled its venv at 08:50, consistent with preemption and reschedule on the preemptible v4 pool.
- Distinct from the wait-budget overruns in #8580, #8529, and #8273: this job failed at 1h16m, well under the 7100s wait budget.

## Canary run context

- Lane: datakit-smoke (Tier 1, TPU / GCP)
- Iris job ID: `/runner/iris-run-job-20260824-073906`
- GHA run: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/32702408963
- Run ID: `datakit-smoke-32702408963-1`
- W&B: `marin-community/marin` (datakit smoke does not create a per-run W&B run)
- Date: 2026-08-24

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
The expert-parallel ring MoE backend (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py`, `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local`) computes wrong outputs. Against an exact fp32 dense MoE reference on a GB200 node with mesh `(data=2, expert=2, model=1)`, E=8 experts (4 per shard), top-2, 64 tokens/device, H=64, I=96, bf16, capacity factor 2.0 (both implementations report zero drops), ring's forward deviates by 0.75x-0.93x relative on most seeds and produced values of magnitude 2.3e28 on one seed; its gradients contain NaN. The ragged all-to-all backend on identical inputs matches the dense reference to 0.4-0.5% (bf16 noise) with clean gradients, so the harness and inputs are not the cause. This matters because ring is the implementation other backends are validated against (`test_moe_mlp_ragged_matches_ring_with_ep_axis_when_available` skips on CPU, so the EP path is effectively untested in CI).

A second defect: at capacity factor 4.0 in the same configuration, `jax.lax.top_k(selection_key, local_capacity)` at `ep_ring.py:88` requests k=512 from a 256-row selection pool and crashes; `local_capacity` is not capped at the gathered pool size.

Reproduce:
1. On branch `research/mcwitt/8317-ragged-tune`, submit `python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.ragged_ep_check --version dev --run` (needs 4 GB200s; the check compares ring, ragged, and the exact dense reference).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

I reproduced both defects on current `main` with four GB200s. At capacity 2.0, ring had 0 drops but forward relative max error was 0.79, 0.90, 0.96, and 1.93 across seeds 0–3; seed 1 produced non-finite gradients. Forcing `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla` reduced those errors to 0.005–0.007 with finite gradients, isolating the corruption to the Triton ragged-dot kernel: its physical power-of-two tiles read and write past logical M/N/K boundaries. Capacity 4.0 separately requests `top_k(k=512)` from 256 rows.

**Relevant code**
- [`ragged_dot.py#L103-L135`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L103-L135) - unmasked forward tiles
- [`ragged_dot.py#L179-L210`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L179-L210) - unmasked weight-gradient tiles
- [`ep_ring.py#L56-L88`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L56-L88) - uncapped selection capacity
- [`test_grugformer_moe.py#L957-L1012`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py#L957-L1012) - ring used as oracle

# Proposed Fix

Mask edge reads and writes in both Triton ragged-dot layouts, and cap ring's selection capacity at the gathered assignment pool size. Replace ring-as-oracle coverage with value and gradient comparisons against a direct dense `einsum` MoE reference; retain backend-to-backend checks only as secondary diagnostics. Exercise ring at excess capacity to cover the crash, and validate the portable ring, ragged all-to-all, fixed all-to-all, and pooled-wave paths against the dense reference where their runtimes are available.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body: 🤖 Draft fix: #8610. Masking logical Triton tile boundaries reduced ring's four-seed GB200 forward error from 0.79–1.93 to 0.005–0.007, restored finite gradients within 0.006 of the fp32 dense reference, and made capacity factor 4.0 succeed. EP tests now use a direct dense MoE oracle; ring, fixed all-to-all, and pooled-wave have cross-shard value/gradient coverage, while ragged runs the same check on supported accelerator runtimes. Current `main` still segfaults inside XLA's ragged all-to-all on stock GB200 before parity can be measured, and DeepEP's external FFI transport remains outside portable end-to-end tests.

issues.author: marianna13
issues.body: # Hypothesis / goal H0: Short RL training (<200 steps) cannot teach a task-specific skill but only re-usable skills (e.g. using agentic harness). H1: RL does teach task-specific skills. # Method Definitions: - We call transferrable (or re-usable skills) a capabilities that can be applied to different tasks and do not depend on the specific task context. Examples: tool usage, efficient context usage etc. - On the other hand, the skills that are only useful for specific tasks we will call task-specific. They help with certain tasks/contexts but cannot be applied universally and therefore are not helpful in general. To determine whether RL only teaches transferrable skills we conduct following experiments: - Exp 1: RL on the non-agentic base. Non-agentic model is not familiar with the specific harness, so RL needs to teach this capability first. If RL is capable of pushing task-specific skill further we should see continuous improvement in pass@1 (reward). However, if RL only teaches how to use the harness we would expect rising reward in the beginning and then plateau (model effectively learned how to use the harness but it doesn't improve in actual task solution and RL exhausted what it can squeeze from the policy). Note: this does not mean that it's the case (it can be something else like exploration collapse) but it's one evidence that will count towards H0. Therefore, exp 1 on it's own is not enough to disprove H1. - Exp 2: RL on agentic base (already knows how to use the harness). Evidence for H1: reward should climb - RL can teach capability beyond harness usage. If reward is flat it's another evidence towards H0. - Exp 3: RL on agentic base with a different harness. If H0 holds, the behavior should be similar to Exp 1 - reward rises up in the beginning and thne plateaus. - Exp 4: RL that rewards transferrable skills beyond harness usage. Construct tasks that require some re-usable skill in order to solve and reward the model for efficient usage of that skill. Rising reward here would also support H0 (though is not a clear evidence against H1). All together Exp. 1-4 should provide enough evidence to prove or disprove H0. We don't test RL transfer (i.e. agent performance on OOD tasks) since we only care about training dynamics and the transfer is a separate question. # Status In the process of consolidating the empirical evidence. ## Exp 1 Qwen3-8B (no agentic) on [code-contests](https://huggingface.co/datasets/DCAgent/code-contests-noblock) dataset and terminus-2 harness. We see rapid increase in training reward in just 15 steps in the beginning and then a plateau. This behavior is consistent with "the non-agentic model first learned how to use the harness and how to behave in the agentic workflows". Then RL just stops being useful. For comparison, I also did the same setup but [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) (agentic SFT on top of Qwen3-8B). We see that for SFT'ed model there's no improvement (even a small decrease) in reward where the base was improving. Importantly, g1 starts where base finishes (0.30 -> 0.50 by step 15). However, both improve their token efficiency (base -10% and g1 -15% in avg response length), this is supports H0 - a systematic behavioral skill that RL can teach a model. ## Exp 2 Ran [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) (Qwen3-8B trained on teacher traces with terminus-2 harness) on R2E-Gym dataset with ctx len 81k (yarn factor=2). Harness: terminus-2 (t2) - native for g1. Longer context was used because for r2e tasks and terminus-2 more than half of rollouts are useless - they crash with CLE. Trained for 84 steps. Reward over 84 steps: 0.326->0.375, p@8: 0.516->0.609. The reward slope shrinks from +0.00086 to +0.00032/step as more steps are added (a plateau), not a slow climb that just needed room. pass@8 is visibly pinned at ~0.60 from step 10 onward. There's areal policy movement shown by KL climbing but almost no improvement in pass rate. ## Exp 3 Same configuration as Exp 2 but with terminus-structured harness and native 40k ctx len for Qwen (t-struct has better context management than t2 ). Trained for 140 steps. Reward over 140 steps: 0.24 -> 0.35 (almost the same p@1 as g1 on t2 starts from i.e. no real capability gain). p@: 0.47->0.58 (again g1 t2 starts at 0.58). ## Exp 4 [g1](https://huggingface.co/DCAgent/g1_diverse_tezos_100k_8b) on [SWE-smith-py-code-search](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenHands/SWE-smith-py-code-search). The task is code localization and not bug fixes. The reward function is $R=R^{F1-file}+R^{F1-module}+R^{F1-entity}$ sum of F1 scores for each granularity (file-, module-, entity-based localization). We see that for g1 the reward monotonically grows - the model learns to efferently search and at the same time becomes more efficient (avg response length drops). For each granularity level, we see that entity-level is the hardest and the steepest while file-level is almost saturated. Interestingly entity-level continues # Links - consolidated logs (Claude-generated): [link](https://huggingface.co/datasets/laion/rl-analysis-issue-8481) # Conclusion In all RL runs where reward is growing we see similar behavior - first it goes up and then plateaus. All exp.1-4 provide support for H0 and there's no counterexample. So we don't have enough evidence to reject H0 so

## Summary

The [GPU nightly](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/actions/runs/32187801965) is false-green on `cccab723`.

`setuptools-scm` cannot parse the nearest Marin release tag. Because version resolution runs inside `echo`, the workflow continues with an empty `SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION`. The no-`.git` Iris bundle then fails to build vLLM.

Iris reports `JOB_STATE_FAILED`, but `iris ... | tee nightly.log` returns `tee`'s successful status. GitHub therefore reports success and skips automated failure reporting. Reusing the same Iris job name also mixes older successful output into the current log.

This happened in every scheduled run from August 15–18. The [August 14 run](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/actions/runs/31794329673) was the last genuine pass.

Related: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8323

## Acceptance criteria

- Produce a non-empty, PEP 440-valid version with existing Marin tags, or fail before requesting a GPU.
- Propagate Iris failures through log capture while still uploading the log.
- Keep Iris jobs and logs specific to each GitHub run.
- Add cheap regression coverage for version resolution and pipeline failure propagation.
- Rerun the fixing head on H100 and confirm both Iris and GitHub report success.

issues.author: weaverbot
issues.body:
StepRunner can build and execute a graph whose primary GCS storage is in a different region from the Iris root task. The mismatch silently moves bulk parquet data across regions.

Reproduce:
1. Launch a ferry without `--region` and set `MARIN_PREFIX` to `gs://marin-us-central1/...`.
2. Let Iris place the root task in `us-central2`; child jobs inherit that placement.
3. Run a pipeline that reads and writes paths under `MARIN_PREFIX`.

Two recent runs exercised this path: `ab-mapgroupsv3-ae13b5c-08081208` ran 924 task attempts in `us-central2` against `gs://marin-us-central1/infra/datakit/ferry_perf`, and `polars-shuffle-rledyn-fixed-20260807-220745` ran 677 attempts in `us-central2` against `gs://marin-us-central1/tmp/ttl=1d/polars-shuffle-compare-20260807-220745`.

Expected: before submitting data-processing children, StepRunner compares the runtime region with the regions of `MARIN_PREFIX` and primary GCS input/output paths. A mismatch fails with the worker region and offending paths. Intentional cross-region jobs can proceed only through an explicit command-line flag or environment variable override; override use is logged and emitted in telemetry.

Tests should cover matching regions, a mismatch that fails before child submission, and a mismatch allowed by the explicit override.

Related: #3981.

@weaverbot please work on this.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Yes. I recommend rescoping this away from a StepRunner graph guard and to the Iris launch boundary.

I found six non-test Python writes to `MARIN_PREFIX`:

- `experiments/datakit/testbed/{baseline,decon_arm,variants}.py` default to `gs://marin-us-central1`. This keeps the testbed sample, eval corpus, and outputs in their staging region, but it runs after Iris has already placed the root task. These should be removed. The scripts should require/validate `us-central1` at startup using the existing `check_path_in_region` pattern, and their launch examples should pass `--region us-central1`. A correctly placed GCP root already derives `gs://marin-us-central1` from metadata.
- `experiments/ferries/{datakit_ferry,datakit_nemotron_ferry}.py` set it to `marin_temp_bucket(ttl_days=1)` only to put relative outputs under lifecycle-managed storage. This is region-local, but mutating the global prefix is unnecessary. Build their absolute per-run `base` from a local temp-prefix value instead. The Nemotron ferry should retain its existing `check_path_in_region` call for the fixed multi-TB input.
- `experiments/ferries/datakit_tier2_skewed_ferry.py` writes `marin_prefix()` back into the environment. That assignment is redundant; `prefix = marin_prefix()` has the same behavior.

The `MARIN_PREFIX` values in CoreWeave `defaults.task_env` are different: they are cluster storage configuration, needed because those workers do not have GCP metadata and each cluster has a specific S3 endpoint/bucket. Those should stay. Per-job `-e MARIN_PREFIX ...` in workflows and launch examples that merely repeat the CoreWeave default can go. GCP smoke configuration that starts a single-region test cluster, and the GCP canary validator environment that runs outside Iris, are also intentional.

For the contained guard, add a check in `iris job run` after `.marin.yaml` and `-e` values are merged, before submission:

1. If the job does not explicitly set a GCS `MARIN_PREFIX`, allow placement to float.
2. If it does, require an explicit `--region` or `--zone`. Reject an unconstrained launch because Iris may choose another region.
3. Resolve the bucket location and require every allowed region to match it. A repeated `--region` list is safe only if every candidate is co-regional.
4. Allow only an explicit `--allow-cross-region` or job-level `MARIN_I_WILL_PAY_FOR_ALL_FEES`; log the prefix and requested regions when it is used.

`rigging.filesystem.check_path_in_region` supplies most of the mechanism, and the Nemotron ferry is already a concrete caller. The launch check should fail closed if bucket location cannot be determined; the current helper warns and returns on a permission error, which is too weak for this contract.

I would not inspect arbitrary StepSpec dependency paths in this first change. #3981, #3983, and the closed #8138 show the cached-dependency and computation-mobility false positives, while runtime paths inside Polars are not statically visible anyway. Fixed large inputs should use pipeline-specific `check_path_in_region` calls.

The focused tests are: unset prefix permits an unpinned launch; matching prefix/region permits submission; explicit prefix with no placement fails before submission; mismatch fails; zone-derived match passes; and the explicit override permits the mismatch and logs it.

issues.author: RohithKuditipudi
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**
TPU v4 workers fail when the vLLM/TorchAX TPU path reaches ragged paged attention v3:

```text
NotImplementedError: Unsupported tpu_version=4
```

The failure appeared on `v4-8` pools in xregion joint-decode evals. Non-v4 pools continue past this point, so this is a v4 kernel-support issue rather than a general install failure.

**To Reproduce**
1. Run a vLLM/TorchAX TPU generation workload on a `v4-8` Iris worker.
2. Use the default TPU attention path, which selects `FLASH_ATTN`.
3. Start decoding so the common attention interface calls RPA v3.

**Expected behavior**
`v4-8` workers should either run with conservative v4-safe RPA v3 block sizes or fail earlier with a clear unsupported-platform message before scheduling production eval chunks there.

**Additional context**
The current path is `FLASH_ATTN` -> `tpu_inference.layers.common.attention_interface` -> `tpu_inference.kernels.ragged_paged_attention.v3.kernel`.

`tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py:get_default_block_sizes` handles TPU versions `5 | 6` and `7`, then raises for everything else. `v3/tuned_block_sizes.py` already has a conservative TPU v4 fallback, so the minimal fix is likely adding a `case 4` to the default v3 heuristic. `USE_BATCHED_RPA_KERNEL=1` may be a diagnostic workaround, but it is explicitly experimental and should not be the default production answer without a v4 smoke.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS.md and skill playbooks
- [x] Check actionability (depends on #5995, several design choices unstated)
- [x] Survey existing zephyr skills and config surface
- [x] Post research + clarifying questions; no PR (design-sized, dep-blocked)

# Research

Two reasons this isn't PR-ready:

1. **Hard dep on #5995.** Bullet 2 ("use the stats from #5995") needs the `zephyr.stage` finelog stream from #5995, which isn't built yet — the proposed approach was just posted there today with open questions. A skill written against stats that don't exist will codify a fake schema. The skew-detection bullet has the same problem at per-shard granularity (`zephyr.shard`), and #5995's current scope explicitly defers per-shard rows.
2. **No definition of done for the skill itself.** The bullets describe *inputs to a heuristic*, not the skill's output, entry point, or scope. Concretely: where does the skill apply its recommendation (config file diff? new job submission? PR comment? chat reply?), what knobs does it touch (`map_workers_per_actor`, `reduce_workers_per_actor`, Iris `--memory`, scatter buffer fractions?), is it pre-job (plan from inputs only) or post-mortem (analyze a finished run) or mid-flight (suggest restart params)?

What's available today vs. what the skill would need:

| Need | Today | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| Shard count from inputs | [`readers.py#L98`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/readers.py#L98) `InputFileSpec`; row/byte ranges already supported | None — can list/size files via gsutil/fsspec |
| Per-stage throughput | [`execution.py#L191-L241`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L191-L241) `_stage_throughput` (in-process only) | Needs #5995 to land for cross-run history |
| Per-shard skew signal | [`OPS.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/OPS.md) "Straggler Detection" — manual via `list-tasks` memoryMb + `actor call get_counters` | No durable per-shard counter stream (#5995 defers `zephyr.shard`) |
| Memory/thread knobs | [`execution.py#L1356`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1356) `map_workers_per_actor` / `reduce_workers_per_actor`; Iris `--memory` on `job run` | None |

**Relevant code**
- [`readers.py#L98-L125`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/readers.py#L98-L125) — `InputFileSpec`, the natural shard unit
- [`execution.py#L1356-L1416`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1356-L1416) — worker-slot knobs the skill would tune
- [`shuffle.py#L138-L142`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py#L138-L142) — scatter buffer is `memory / num_workers`, so memory and worker-count tune together
- [`OPS.md` — Straggler Detection / Data Skew](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/OPS.md) — already documents the manual procedure a skill would automate
- [`.agents/skills/babysit-zephyr/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/babysit-zephyr/SKILL.md) and [`evaluate-zephyr-perf/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.agents/skills/evaluate-zephyr-perf/SKILL.md) — style/scope precedents (this skill is the missing third leg: pre-flight planner / post-mortem optimizer)

# Proposed approach (needs sign-off before writing the skill)

Split into two skills along the pre-job / post-job seam, since they use disjoint inputs and produce disjoint outputs:

**A. `plan-zephyr` (pre-job, no #5995 dep).** Input: a submission script or pipeline plan. Skill:
1. Resolves `InputFileSpec`s, enumerates files via fsspec, captures size and (for parquet) row counts.
2. Reports shard count and shard-size distribution (p50/p95/max/skew-ratio).
3. Picks `map_workers_per_actor`, `reduce_workers_per_actor`, and Iris `--memory` from a small heuristic table (e.g. memory = max(scatter-buffer-floor, p95 shard bytes × buffer-multiple); workers = min(cpu_count, p95-shard-mem-fit)).
4. Emits a diff against the user's submission command + a one-paragraph rationale. Does **not** auto-submit.

Doable now. ~100 LOC of skill prose + a small `scripts/zephyr/plan_inputs.py` helper for file enumeration (the heuristic itself stays in the skill prose; agents apply judgment).

**B. `tune-zephyr` (post-mortem, blocked on #5995).** Input: a finished or in-flight `iris_job_id`. Skill:
1. Pulls `zephyr.stage` rows for the run; flags stages where `item_rate` collapsed late (straggler signature) or `peak_worker_memory_mb` was close to allocation (under-provisioned).
2. Cross-references `iris.worker` (already exists) for OOM/preemption.
3. For skew, falls back to manual `actor call get_counters` per OPS.md until #5995 ships `zephyr.shard`.
4. Emits a recommended config delta for the next run, plus a "re-shard the input" recommendation when input skew is the dominant cost.

Out-of-scope for now (flag if you disagree):
- Auto-resubmitting with new params — risky without human review.
- Modifying scatter internals (covered by `evaluate-zephyr-perf`).
- CPU sizing — Iris already sets that per cluster config; not a Zephyr-side knob.

**Questions for @wmoss before I write either skill:**

- **(a) Split A/B or single skill?** I lean two skills (different inputs, different cadences, B blocks on #5995). Push back if you want one entry point.
- **(b) Output channel.** Print to terminal in the invoking chat (like `debug`), comment on a PR (like `evaluate-zephyr-perf`), or write a recommended config file? My default: terminal for A, comment on the issue/PR that owns the run for B.
- **(c) Heuristic provenance.** Do you have an existing rule-of-thumb for memory-per-shard / workers-per-actor I should encode, or should I derive defaults from a few representative ferries (datakit tier1/tier2/tier3) and bake those numbers in?
- **(d) Skew action.** When the skill flags skewed input shards, what's the recommended remediation in this codebase — a `repartition`/`reshuffle` op, manual `InputFileSpec` row-range splits, or just "tell the user and stop"?
- **(e) Defer B until #5995 lands?** Or stub it now against the proposed schema and update when #5995 lands?

Holding off on PRs pending answers, since (b)–(d) materially change the skill's content.

issues.title: [zephyr] Create an agent skill for optimizing a Zephyr job

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
## Description

Build **smallquery**: self-serve, BigQuery-like SQL analytics over our Parquet datasets on object storage (regional GCS and CoreWeave), running on Iris and using spare capacity on preemptible VMs. A user submits a SQL query through an API or dashboard and gets the result back in object storage to stream or download.

Design and implementation notes (the *how*) live in `.agents/projects/smallquery/` and `lib/smallquery/`. This issue tracks the **system requirements**, not the design.

## System requirements

- **Distributed execution with shuffle** — must run joins and high-cardinality `GROUP BY` across many workers, not single-node only. (Hard requirement.)
- **Preemption-tolerant** — workers run on preemptible VMs that can vanish at any moment; a query must still complete with correct results, without restarting from scratch.
- **Scales beyond one node** — handles queries whose working set exceeds a single VM's memory.
- **Opportunistic / good neighbour** — uses spare CPU/RAM and yields to higher-priority work; never starves co-located jobs.
- **Data-local, egress-aware** — computes in the same region/cloud as the data; rejects (or explicitly gates) queries that would cause cross-region egress.
- **Durable results** — materializes the full result to object storage (stream/download) plus a quick, size-capped inline preview.
- **Self-serve access** — a query API and a dashboard reachable on the Iris cluster.
- **Governed access** — datasets referenced by name through a catalog with per-dataset authorization; no raw object-store paths in user SQL (potentially integrated with the artifact registry).
- **Correct** — results match a single-node reference engine over the same data.

## Dependencies

- A per-node worker-fleet capability on Iris (#6763).

## Definition of Done (capabilities)

- [ ] A join and a high-cardinality `GROUP BY` run **distributed** and return correct results.
- [ ] Killing workers mid-query does not fail or corrupt the query — it still returns the correct result.
- [ ] Runs on spare/preemptible capacity and yields to higher-priority jobs.
- [ ] Results land in object storage and are reachable via the API + dashboard on both GCS and CoreWeave.
- [ ] Cross-region queries are rejected or explicitly gated per the egress policy.
- [ ] Results validated equal to a single-node reference.
- [ ] Design doc reviewed/merged.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
The option in one picture: a persistent non-preemptible coordinator (API + dashboard) + a fleet of warm preemptible workers; queries become a DAG of shards that exchange chunks through object storage (never local disk); results to a TTL'd location + capped preview.

Key choices — each had a real alternative:
- Distributed + object-store shuffle ↔ single-node big-RAM (evaluated, rejected — distributed was a hard requirement; cf. https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6760)
- Object-store shuffle ↔ local-disk shuffle on an SSD scratch group (would unlock off-the-shelf Spark/Trino).
- New IrisDaemon per-node primitive ↔ standing pool / per-query jobs.
- Per-attempt _SUCCESS manifest committer ↔ atomic-rename / conditional-create.
- Thin coordinator + embedded SQLite snapshotted to GCS ↔ reconcile-by-listing / Postgres.
- Kernel: DataFusion vs DuckDB left as a measured bake-off.
- Python coordinator (logical-plan cutting) + Rust workers ↔ Rust coordinator shipping physical plans.
- Skew: fail cheaply ↔ salting/spill.

Prior art: borrowed finelog (deployment/dashboard/SQLite-checkpoint) and zephyr (object-store scatter, retry tiers); the Spice AI Ballista fork is the only OSS object-store shuffle but recomputes durable data on writer loss (our committer avoids that); ClickHouse/smallpond/Polars rejected for our constraints.

One practically and lazy option would be to borrow useful parts/components of DataFusion/Ballista and sprinkle it with parts that require custom handling.

Worth noting the [limitations of distributed-datafusion](https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/index.html#when-not-to-use-this-library), specifically:
> * If any node fails mid-query, the whole query fails; there are no retries.
> * There’s no persistence of intermediate results, so queries can’t checkpoint or resume from where they stopped.

This is probably fine for the interactive workload, but this is the trap that our preemptable infra sets and it would be worth analyzing query runtime vs. node preemption to see what percentage of queries would fail and at what scale it becomes unusable.

comments.author: alxmrs
comments.body:
Here are my thoughts and impressions about which technology choices to make for the smallquery project: 

## DuckDB vs Polars vs DataFusion

These are all very similar but I think there are some important  differences that will lead us to decide that DataFusion is the right RDBMS engine to build atop of. 

Here is DataFusion's explanation of the differences between each project: https://datafusion.apache.org/user-guide/faq.html#how-does-datafusion-compare-with-xyz

- DuckDB vs DataFusion: Both are very similar in goal (in process/embeddable OLAP query engine). DuckDB is built around its own internal format whereas DataFusion is designed to be agnostic of the core DB format. 
- DuckDB vs DataFusion: Both are modular and extensible, but DataFusion is the natural ancestor to Apache Arrow; see this post on [Composable Data Systems](https://wesmckinney.com/blog/looking-back-15-years/)
- DuckDB vs (DataFusion & Polars): C++ (sometimes, with Rust Extensions) vs a pure-rust ecosystem -- my preference is to go with Rust.
- Polars vs the rest: Polars is built on arrow, but is not designed as a "deconstructed database" like DuckDB and DataFusion, so it will be harder to integrate with. 

## Distribution 

Assuming DataFusion is the bet we go with, the next open question is Comet vs Ballista vs DataFusion Distributed: 

- Comet is DataFusion/Arrow within Spark, so I see this as really saying we should go with (better) Spark. While this is faster than Spark, it is still the slowest option in the distributed DataFusion ecosystem. This is lowest on my list, primarily because it adds a lot of system complexity (I count ~4-5 layers of abstraction between Zephyr, Spark, Comet, DataFusion, and Iris). The benefit, however, is that Comet happened to be a more popular choice than Ballista, even though I think Ballista is a better system. I think this might have to do with the amount of buy-in/popularity of Apache Spark.
- Ballista is the most mature way of distributing DataFusion. However, the DataFusion-Python to Ballista Python integration is somewhat far behind the primary version of DataFusion, making it suspect for us to want to depend on. (Warning: I could be wrong about this impression -- this is from recently trying to build on top of Ballista with Python a few months ago).
- DataFusion-Distributed is the new distributed system for DataFusion, and its core promise is to be a natural extension of the DataFusion data model (logical and physical plans). https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/. I like this choice for Iris because it delegates full control over how plans are distributed over workers, so I think it would give us more power to handle retries and preemption in an iris layer rather than the DB layer. It also should delegate to Iris actors with a more lightweight interface than Ballista. I also like that it looks like this system will be integrated into DataFusion-Python soon: https://github.com/apache/datafusion-python/issues/1612. That said, the concerns that Will pointed out from the "when not to use this section" may be dealbreakers, and the right bet is to integrate Ballista into Iris workers. 

I also just posted in the DataFusion Discord to ask what the maintainers recommend. It might be that the best way to find out would be to build a small prototype with DataFusion.

## Responses to the above discussion

>  still doesn't mean you couldn't use the same distributed sql engine with scheduling similar to Zephyr's today for the larger data processing jobs.
> Why only share the shuffle? Presumably smallquery has would also need to do distributed maps for certain queries?
> there's no reason it couldn't also handle the things written in Python / Zephyr today.

I am 100% on this team; I think a SQL engine is the core thing you need for doing ELT/ETL, even for [non-tabular data](https://github.com/jayendra13/zarr-datafusion).

> How much of this could we reuse from Datafusion/Ballista? It looks like the main gap there would be the shuffles do temp writes to local disk. We could bring some of those ideas in though.

I agree, I think reusing DB technology is better than reinventing it, especially since distributed shuffles for reductions are non-trivial. I think DataFusion-Distributed would fit in the cleanest with Iris, if we can handle retry logic and persistence (maybe that makes Ballista the winner -- my original intention with https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5861 was to have the DataFusion Context be swappable with a Ballista Context running on other workers in Iris). 

> ~100 sources, ~100k parquet files, ~35TB. In most cases we can assume parquet, but other formats would be nice to have.

35 TB is small. If we're looking for Marin Infra to support workloads in scientific applications like Coral, then we'd want to make sure this system scales to the 1s to 10s of petabytes IMO. We don't need to do this now, but it would be nice to know that such a thing is possible. (I still dream of loading all 12 PiBs of [ARCO-ERA5](https://github.com/google-research/arco-era5) into Marin). [Samudra](https://github.com/m2lines/Samudra), my primary project, is still looking for a core data engineering system replacement to Dask, and a 3 PiB dataset is on our roadmap to process.

> at some point I was curious if I could replace that with Arrow/Parquet, do you happen to have experience with that use-case? Scale ~20T. Actually, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4445 would be a good place to have this chat to keep this issue focused.

I'm part of the cult of [zarr.dev](https://zarr.dev), so I think Tensorstore on Zarr or maybe IceChunk is a better fit than parquet for Array shaped data. I think there could be a good opportunity to make a patch or extension to Orbax.

> I think it would probably look more like building sql support into Zephyr
> I'll work on a more coherent / detailed design proposal.

That's the dream. LMK if I can chat with you or collaborate on the design. I've done some work in this space.

comments.author: wmoss
claude[bot]
comments.body:
**Claude finished @wmoss's task in 2m 24s** —— [View job](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/28962455679)

---
### Ballista on Iris — deployment shape & failure model

I dug into how Zephyr deploys on Iris (the pattern you'd copy) and mapped Ballista's components onto it. TL;DR: deploying Ballista on Iris is mechanically easy and looks almost exactly like Zephyr's coordinator+workers; the hard part is exactly the one you flagged — **Ballista shuffles to executor-local disk, so an executor dying after it produced shuffle output forces recompute, and that recompute cascades under preemption.** Details below. I'd love @gabotechs to correct anything I get wrong about current Ballista internals.

---

### 1. The deployment is the easy part — it mirrors Zephyr almost 1:1

Zephyr already does the "scheduler + N executors per query" thing you're describing. One query = one Iris **job** that hosts the coordinator actor in-process and spins up an executor **actor group** as a child:

- `_run_coordinator_job` hosts the coordinator via `client.host_actor(...)` — [`execution.py:1543`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1543)
- executors are a sized child actor group — `client.create_actor_group(ZephyrWorker, ..., count=actual_workers, resources=..., actor_config=ActorConfig(max_task_retries=10))` — [`execution.py:1571`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1571)
- children are cascade-terminated when the coordinator job exits, so no orphaned executors ([`execution.py:6-11`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L4))

The Ballista analog:

| Ballista | Iris mapping |
|---|---|
| `ballista-scheduler` | one long-lived process — either the coordinator job itself, or a co-hosted actor (like Zephyr's in-process coordinator). Put it on the **non-preemptible** coordinator node from the design sketch above. |
| `ballista-executor` × N | a `create_actor_group(count=N)` of executor actors on preemptible workers, each running the executor gRPC server and registering with the scheduler |
| scheduler↔executor gRPC + Arrow Flight shuffle fetch | actor RPC endpoints; executors need to reach each other's Flight ports (Iris already gives every task a routable endpoint) |
| scheduler state store (in-mem / sled / etcd) | see §3 — this is where preemption survival is decided |

So "deploy scheduler + N executors per query" is a thin wrapper: a coordinator entrypoint that boots the scheduler, launches an executor actor group, submits the SQL, and writes results out. Nothing about Iris blocks this.

### 2. Executor failure — what actually happens

This is the crux. Ballista breaks the physical plan into **query stages** at every shuffle boundary. A `ShuffleWriterExec` at the end of a stage writes its output partitions as Arrow IPC files to the **executor's local disk**; the next stage's `ShuffleReaderExec` pulls those partitions from the producing executor over Arrow Flight.

Two distinct failure cases:

1. **Executor dies while running a task** → the scheduler sees the task fail / the executor heartbeat lapse, and reschedules that task onto another executor. This is fine — recompute one task from durable source data. Iris bringing up a replacement (the `max_task_retries` behavior) lines up with this; the new executor re-registers with the scheduler, just like Zephyr workers re-register after reconstruction ([`execution.py:351`](lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L351)).

2. **Executor dies *after* it finished a stage, and a downstream stage still needs its shuffle output** → that shuffle data was on local disk and is now **gone**. A reader hits a *fetch failure*. Ballista's recovery here is Spark-style: mark the lost shuffle partitions, and **re-run the map task(s) that produced them** (potentially the whole producing stage). Because the ultimate inputs are parquet in object storage, this is *recoverable in principle* — but under continuous preemption it **cascades**: re-running a producing stage means its executors write new shuffle files… which can also be lost before they're consumed. Query wall-time balloons; at enough scale/preemption rate the success probability collapses exactly as you predicted.

So the answer to "if an executor fails and Iris brings up another one, what happens?": the *running task* recovers cleanly, but any *already-materialized shuffle output on the dead node is lost and must be recomputed*, and that recompute is where preemption bites.

This is precisely why the design comment upthread proposes an **object-store shuffle with a per-attempt `_SUCCESS` committer** instead: once a stage's shuffle output is committed to GCS/CoreWeave, losing the executor costs you *nothing* — the durable partitions are still there, and a replacement executor just reads them. That's the property Zephyr already has (shuffle chunks live in the chunk store / object storage, not local disk), and it's the single most important thing Ballista does **not** give you out of the box.

### 3. Scheduler failure — does the whole query die?

Depends on the scheduler's state backend:

- **In-memory state (default single-scheduler)**: scheduler death = all job/stage/task state lost = **the query dies and cannot resume**. Restarting gives you a blank scheduler. This is the mode most people run.
- **Persistent state backend (sled embedded, or etcd in older versions)**: job graph and task/stage status are persisted, so a restarted scheduler can in principle recover in-flight jobs. In practice this path has historically been the less-exercised one, and it still doesn't rescue the lost *local-disk shuffle data* from §2 — it only rescues the *control-plane* state.

For Marin this means: keep the scheduler on the **non-preemptible** coordinator node (it's tiny — one per query), so scheduler loss is not a normal event. Then all the "can we survive preemption" weight lands on the executors, and the executor story only works if shuffle is durable (§2). Note this is a strictly *better* position than [datafusion-distributed's documented stance](https://datafusion-contrib.github.io/datafusion-distributed/index.html#when-not-to-use-this-library) ("any node fails → whole query fails; no retries; no intermediate persistence") — Ballista at least *has* task reschedule + shuffle-recompute, which is why @gabotechs is steering you to Ballista over datafusion-distributed for the preemption constraint.

### 4. Net assessment for the smallquery constraint

- **Deploying Ballista on Iris**: straightforward, copy the Zephyr coordinator/executor-group pattern.
- **Executor preemption**: survivable but *expensive* out-of-the-box because of local-disk shuffle → recompute cascade. The fix is durable (object-store) shuffle output — the same thing the design notes and @rjpower/@wmoss's "reusable shuffle lib" thread are circling.
- **Scheduler preemption**: pin the scheduler to the non-preemptible node; don't rely on Ballista HA state recovery for the common case.

Concretely, if you want to validate the failure math you asked for, the cheapest experiment is: run a single distributed join on Ballista-on-Iris, kill an executor **after** its shuffle-producing stage completes but **before** the consuming stage reads it, and measure (a) does it recover, (b) how much recompute it costs. That directly exercises the §2 case and tells you whether default Ballista is viable or whether the object-store-shuffle swap is mandatory before this is usable on preemptible capacity.

I kept this to analysis (no code changes) since the ask was to look into feasibility. Happy to prototype the coordinator/executor-group wrapper or the kill-an-executor test harness if you want to turn this into a spike.
 · branch `claude/issue-6761-20260708-1728`

comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
Thanks @ravwojdyla, now I feel like I better understand what use cases we want to support.

@alxmrs I agree that DataFusion feels like the right solution here and I think Ballista is the only reasonable choice.

If we want to support long-running / large jobs, I think we need to use GCS for checkpointing stage output instead of local disk. Otherwise I think the intersection of long processing times, lots of workers and those workers getting preempted is going to kill job performance or worse, make it never finish.

I had Gemini do an analysis of having Ballista checkpoint to GCS (attached) and it was actually somewhat promising. The main things I was worried about was that Ballista would likely create a lot of small files from the shuffle, which it does out of the box, but it also supports a sort-based shuffle that writes one large file and has reducers seek into it (this is what Zephyr does). I'm less worried than Gemini about the cost of updating all the call sites to support object storage since I think AI's costing models are generally based on pre-AI costs. It also seems like something that we could, hopefully, commit back to Ballista, since I definitely don't want to be maintaining a long-running fork.

As a first PoC, my suggestion would actually be to use `gcsfuse` to mount a GCS bucket to the local filesystem. It will certainly be less performant than changing the Ballista code, but wouldn't actually require any code changes to Ballista to get something up and running just to see if it works. 

@alxmrs, I'm going to take over from Rav on the infra side here, but if you're stoked on this feel free to take a crack at it and I'm happy to collaborate. Otherwise I can point an AI at it and see how far it can get, but I've got plenty to keep me busy so you're welcome to run with it.

  - xref: https://github.com/jja725/ballista-riffle
  - xref: https://github.com/spiceai/datafusion-ballista

I think the fastest, most dependable path forward would be to depend or contribute to their fork, or the existing datafusion-contrib projects that aim to push this upstream (maybe, each of these paths could be guarded by a feature flag?).

comments.body:
> One major technical note: SpiceAI already has a fork that we could adopt that would make Ballista work better for shuffles in our environment, see -- https://spice.ai/blog/apache-ballista-at-spice-ai

Maybe I'm missing something, but from what I can see, they didn't do anything with shuffle. comments.author: wmoss
comments.body:
🤖 **Status update: Distributed DataFusion-Ballista PoC & Comparison on Iris**

We stood up a DataFusion-Ballista distributed scheduler and executor pool on-Iris and evaluated its performance against the standard Zephyr pipeline for the text normalization step. See the [draft PR #7588](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7588) and the [detailed subissue #7266 comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7266#issuecomment-5065971169) for more information.

| Metric | Zephyr Pipeline | Ballista Pipeline (Optimized) | Speedup / Reduction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Normalize Step Time** | **1h 20m 24s** (80.4 min) | **5m 33s** (5.5 min) | **14.4× faster** |
| **Overall Wall Time** | 1h 20m 47s | 5m 33s (non-concurrent mode) | **14.5× faster** |
| **GCS Scan / Read Count** | 1 pass (6 GB read) | 1 pass per query (288 GB total scanned) | ~48× increase (sequential planning) |
| **Output File Correctness** | 22 parquet shards | 22 parquet shards | Identical shard count & schemas |

---

### ⚠️ Critical Downsides & Limitations of Ballista

While the raw execution speed is a massive improvement, we identified severe developer and scalability limitations when compared to Zephyr:

1. **No Distributed Python UDFs**: Remote executors cannot deserialize and run Python objects. This meant we were *unable* to implement the existing Zephyr logic exactly; many things had to be changed to similar SQL patterns (e.g., native regexp/hash/string expressions). Expressing these complex transformations in SQL results in highly nested, verbose query strings that are difficult to read and make the control flow opaque.
2. **No native Gzip NdJson/CSV support (`json.gz`)**: Ballista remote executors cannot parse gzipped raw formats. This means we could not directly process existing Nemotron files without first decompressing or converting them.
3. **Query Planning & Scan Duplication (Sharding Overhead)**: Zephyr handles sharding in-memory in a single pass. Ballista requires planning and submitting $2 \times N_{shards}$ separate SQL queries concurrently. Because each query filters rows using a hash (e.g. `WHERE hash(id) % 22 = i`), executors must scan the raw dataset once per query. On a full-scale dataset (e.g., 4,136 shards), coordinating 8,272 queries would cause planning overhead and total scanned bytes to explode.
