issues.author: muchanem
issues.body:
Relevant work: #6521, [MATES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06046), [Group-MATES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14709), [RegMix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01492v2), [RegMix-D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18663), [Meta-rater](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.14194), [DataMan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19363), [Scalable Influence and Fact Tracing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17413), [DoGE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15393v2)

tl;dr: We should label our data on a bunch of axes (downstream performance, LLM oracle, gradient alignment, etc) and cluster over those axes (and domain) to create buckets for the data mixing swarms

The literature on pre-training data selection has moved fairly significantly beyond FineWeb-Edu style pipelines where you use an LLM-as-judge to rate a sample set of your pretraining data and then train a small model to predict those scalar labels across your pretraining data. 

The first and most important change is treating quality as a multi-dimensional label. In DataMan 14 quality criteria and 15 domains labels are used; in Meta-rater data is labeled on professionalism, readability, reasoning, and cleanliness and proxy models are trained to learn the most useful combination of the signals for validation loss. A scale-up of this approach looks like [propella-1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12414v1)--Qwen3 models which produce structured JSON over 18 properties in six categories. 

The second change is moving to approaches that don't rely on an LLM oracle like downstream performance or gradient alignment. This changes include the further insight that these labels are dynamic (treating each label as conditional on training state/progress). For instance, MATES calculates loss of a model at step t after training on candidate points. DoGE calculates a gradient alignment for full domain buckets.

New work on pretraining data selection has also emphasized the importance of diversity and group-level view of utility. Group-MATES shows that the influence scores of documents cannot be considered independently, and groups documents using their individual influence scores. [Spokes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15216) emphasizes the importance of diversity as a set-level attribute, meaning that buckets themselves should likely get labels as well.

The goal then is a vector of labels per training document, which then get clustered into groups, which can be selected over by our swarms.

Our particular setting and fusing the prior work into one pipeline introduces a few questions but also resolves a few difficulties:
* We are only trying to produce buckets: Meta-rater and Group-MATES think about both the labels and how to select over the labels, we only need to produce the most informative labels possible
* We will/do have training trajectories from model trained over substantially similar data to (presumably) what we will train on in the future. This potentially gives us more signal for model-based labels. However, naively using our checkpoints introduces the danger of only incorporating a memorization/exposure signal rather than a data property itself
* Should our clusters be independent of domain or include domain as another label? (my prior is domain should be included to create clusters)
* The cost and "unity" of the labeler:
   * We could do something like propella-1 where we have a fairly large model predict our entire vector at once. However, this means we introduce a large global barrier into quality labeling work: we can get labels once all have been finalized and the labeler is trained<sup>*</sup>. Additionally, we introduce ~5,000 B200-GPU hours of cost (1B labeler, FP4) to label our training set
   * Alternatively, we train models for each axis we care about at ~the size of our current quality labeler (40M). This allows work on axes to not block each other, but at 20 axes (pessimistically 12 due to small model MFUs) we end up using the same number of GPU hours, for a presumably worse result than predicting all axes at once with a larger model


\* Something like training LoRAs per axis and folding them into the model as we add new axes could work as we expand our set of labels, but also means introducing additional risk as we are stacking multiple bets at once when moving to this approach

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body: As a straw man, what info would you think this would capture that we can't capture from an affine projection from the embeddings we have from Harrier?

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body: A lot of the information is probably directly linearly decodable from the embeddings and doesn't require training a separate model (e.g. for the quality labels, like 90% of the performance of our current model can be captured by a linear probe on the document embedding). But, it's important that the projection be learned--the dominant variance in the embeddings is topic/genre, and so clustering on the embeddings directly (or after a random projection) wouldn't recover things like the MATES downstream performance metric or gradient alignment. So the labels can be understood as making the axes we care about dominant under the clustering metric rather than averaged out. I do also suspect some axes may also turn out to have no signal above label noise in Harrier at all, so we would need to train a separate model.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
Sounds good! Yeah, I think the baseline would be to try your workflow for quality on other axes we care about and only expand to a custom model for axes we have high confidence & evidence will lead to improvements.

The fact that the expensive compute isn't re-usable is what I don't like about the Propella approach. If every time you want to add a new axis you need to re-run a full Qwen model pass over all your data, you'll quickly find yourself avoiding adding new axes because it's expensive and we're unlikely to get the axes right from the get go!

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
I am not well-read in datamixing literature and what actually works- but just a general thought on optimization.

In any open-ended optimization problem, a big decision is how to coalesce the search space into a tractable number of degrees of freedom (EG should we have a learning rate per parameter, or one global LR, or a learning rate per parameter per step). 

To me, every degree of freedom is inherently a bad thing. It exponentially grows the search space, increases risk of overfitting, and makes it harder to interpret results. And it is only worth including a degree of freedom when it empirically proves its worth. I also find it easy to underestimate the future inertia that degrees of freedom introduce. (EG if we fit a unique LR to MLP up projection, suddenly moving to Latent MoE means there is a lot more work to do to retune).

On DataMan 14 quality criteria, my first thought would be "how many of these can we remove without significantly hurting performance". I think its great to test a very large number of hypothesis during exploration phase, but afterwards, every degree of freedom of the system should be sensitive to the objective function- otherwise it should be pruned. I think its easy to get into the reverse mindset, where degrees of freedom are viewed as implying sophistication of the system (but I think this is backwards).

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body: I largely agree--I think the final design will include a step of clustering over all (or all but domain) of the axes, so our search space should stay small and ideally reducing risk of overfitting. However, even in this case we've reduced interpretability a lot, since each bucket is now an "agglomeration of a bunch of factors we think might be relevant" as opposed to something clean like "high quality agent transcripts". I think selecting our axes by how much they change our clustering might be a good approach to maintaining discipline on the number of degrees of freedom we introduce!

Echo's normal Pulumi rollout fails before `migrate.py` starts, while GitHub Actions refreshes its federated credential. The migration subprocess sets `GOOGLE_CLOUD_QUOTA_PROJECT=hai-gcp-models`. Google Auth applies that quota project to the source external-account credential before service-account impersonation completes, so IAM Credentials checks `serviceusage.services.use` on the GitHub `main` Workload Identity principal while minting the deployment token.

PR #8612 granted Service Usage Consumer to the impersonated deployment service account. The [exact merged-main rollout](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/32746184806) still failed with `USER_PROJECT_DENIED` before migration and changed no Echo resources. This isolates the remaining check to the source principal. Echo's API and sync job remain healthy; the [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/228) contains the operational history.

Reproduce:
1. Dispatch `Ops - Pulumi Rollout` from `main` with `service=echo`.
2. Observe `command:local:Command migrate` fail while acquiring impersonated credentials:

   ```text
   USER_PROJECT_DENIED: Caller does not have required permission to use project hai-gcp-models.
   Grant roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer or serviceusage.services.use.
   ```

Expected: the workflow mints the deployment token, applies pending migrations, and completes.

- Marin's canonical IAM data grants `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer` to the exact `marin-community/marin` `main` WIF principal.
- A reviewed `marin` stack apply creates that member.
- An exact-main Echo rollout completes migration, and the API and sync job remain Ready.

```text
principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/748532799086/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github-pool/subject/repo:marin-community/marin:ref:refs/heads/main
```

This is an additive project IAM grant. It does not change Echo's application, migration, scheduler, or workflow logic, and it does not require an index rebuild.

</details>

issues.author: jamt9000
issues.body:
As of #7820 the expert FF parameters are stored in a big `[n_layers, n_experts, d_in, d_out]` tensor, eg `[48, 384, 3072, 3072]`, with the specialised [`_newtonschulz_4d_distributed`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L211) computing Newton Schulz on the last two dimensions.

However, in the optimizer, the axes used to compute the norm will end up as `(1,2,3)`, which includes the expert dimension.

https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py#L76

This seems to be unintentional, since that optimizer code was originally to handle 3D `[n_experts, d_in, d_out]` shapes in #6153.

The implication is that an updated matrix parameter **M**<sub>t+1</sub> will **no longer be constrained to its original hypersphere** of norm ||**M**<sub>t</sub>||<sub>F</sub> as described in MuonH originally. Instead the combined cat([**M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...]) will be constrained to norm ||cat([**M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...])||<sub>F</sub> allowing individual matrices to grow or shrink within that constraint. Although not necessarily a terrible thing to do (experiments in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5253 tried both for AdamH).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Great find. Yes, this is unintentional. Given that our prior tests across 4 scales showed negligible impact (actually slightly better) with norm computation over all experts at once, will leave in and let the run continue.

issues.title: MuonH implementation includes the Expert dimension in the frobenius norm computation for 4D inputs

issues.author: wmoss
issues.body: `lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py` had grown to a lot of lines and also making it hard to avoid circular imports. We should break it up at least into separate files for ZephyrController and ZephyrWorker, but more files might be useful.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and analyze `lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py` (2067 lines)
- [x] Map circular-import surface (`runners.py`, `counters.py`, in-function imports)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight
- [x] Propose split layout

# Research

`execution.py` is 2067 lines holding 5 distinct concerns: shared types/helpers, the worker-side context/protocol surface, [`ZephyrCoordinator`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L431) (~795 lines), [`ZephyrWorker`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1225) (~292 lines), the coordinator-job entrypoint, and [`ZephyrContext`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1730) (~242 lines). The circular-import smell is concrete: [`_default_stage_runner_factory_for`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L393) does in-function imports of \`InlineRunner\`/\`SubprocessRunner\` because [\`runners.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/runners.py#L46-L59) imports types and helpers from \`execution\`, and [\`counters.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/counters.py#L26) reaches in for \`_worker_ctx_var\`.

**Relevant code**
- [\`execution.py#L83-L323\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L83-L323) — shared types (\`PickleDiskChunk\`, \`CounterSnapshot\`, \`TaskResult\`) + formatting/path/IO helpers
- [\`execution.py#L326-L410\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L326-L410) — worker-facing surface (\`WorkerContext\`, \`StageRunner\`, \`ShardTask\`, \`_worker_ctx_var\`)
- [\`execution.py#L431-L1223\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L431-L1223) — \`ZephyrCoordinator\` (note: issue says \"ZephyrController\"; the actual class is \`ZephyrCoordinator\`)
- [\`execution.py#L1225-L1515\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1225-L1515) — \`ZephyrWorker\`
- [\`execution.py#L1579-L1726\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L1579-L1726) — coordinator-job entrypoint (\`_CoordinatorJobConfig\`, \`_run_coordinator_job\`)

# Conflict warning

PR #5814 (\`wmoss/multiprocess-zephyr-workers\`, +362/-282) is open and rewrites large chunks of \`execution.py\`, including \`ZephyrWorker\`. A pure-refactor PR landing first will force a near-total rebase of #5814. Recommend sequencing: land #5814, then do this refactor. Filing the plan now so it doesn't get lost.

# Proposed split

Convert \`zephyr/execution.py\` into a package \`zephyr/execution/\`:

\`\`\`
zephyr/execution/
  __init__.py        # re-export public symbols only (WorkerContext,
                     #   ZephyrContext, ZephyrExecutionResult,
                     #   CounterSnapshot, zephyr_worker_ctx)
  types.py           # ShardFailureKind, PickleDiskChunk, CounterSnapshot,
                     #   TaskResult, ShardTask, WorkerState, JobStatus,
                     #   ZephyrWorkerError, ZephyrExecutionResult,
                     #   _NON_RETRYABLE_ERRORS, ZEPHYR_STAGE_* constants
  worker_context.py  # WorkerContext, _worker_ctx_var, zephyr_worker_ctx,
                     #   StageRunner Protocol
  formatting.py      # _generate_execution_id, _format_count,
                     #   _format_bytes, _stage_throughput,
                     #   _shared_data_path, _push_iris_task_status,
                     #   _cleanup_execution, _write_pickle_chunks,
                     #   _write_stage_output, MAX_STATUS_TEXT_LENGTH
  coordinator.py     # ZephyrCoordinator, _regroup_result_refs,
                     #   MAX_SHARD_FAILURES, MAX_SHARD_INFRA_FAILURES
  worker.py          # ZephyrWorker
  coordinator_job.py # _CoordinatorJobConfig, _run_coordinator_job,
                     #   _read_coordinator_result, _try_read_coordinator_result,
                     #   _default_stage_runner_factory_for
  context.py         # ZephyrContext, _reshard_refs,
                     #   _build_source_shards, _compute_tasks_from_shards,
                     #   _get_stage_description, _print_plan
\`\`\`

Dependency direction (each module imports only from the left):

\`types\` → \`worker_context\` → \`formatting\` → {\`coordinator\`, \`worker\`} → \`coordinator_job\` → \`context\`

Wins:
- \`runners.py\` imports become \`from zephyr.execution.types import …\` / \`from zephyr.execution.worker_context import …\` — no more circular import, in-function imports in [\`_default_stage_runner_factory_for\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L393-L410) can move to module scope.
- \`counters.py\` imports \`_worker_ctx_var\` from \`worker_context\` (leaf module, no \`fray\`/\`iris\` deps).
- \`ZephyrCoordinator\` (~800 LOC) and \`ZephyrWorker\` (~290 LOC) get their own files, matching the issue request.

Per AGENTS.md \"NO BACKWARD COMPATIBILITY\": update all call sites instead of leaving a shim. The package's \`__init__.py\` only re-exports the genuine public surface used by \`zephyr/__init__.py\`; private symbols (\`_worker_ctx_var\`, \`ShardTask\`, \`TaskResult\`, \`CounterSnapshot\`, etc.) imported by [\`runners.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/runners.py#L46-L59), [\`counters.py\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/counters.py#L26), and tests get rewritten to import from the leaf module that owns them.

Call sites to rewrite (from \`grep \"from zephyr.execution\"\`): \`zephyr/__init__.py\`, \`zephyr/runners.py\`, \`zephyr/counters.py\`, \`zephyr/dataset.py\` (docstrings only), 8 \`tests/*\` files, and \`lib/levanter/tests/test_new_cache.py\`.

comments.body:
🤖 [Design artifact](https://loom.oa.dev/s/q4ou0139/artifacts/design)

# Rename `zephyr.execution` to `zephyr.context`

_Research effort: low (issue #5850, PRs #7145 and #5910, the current source tree, Echo, and open-PR preflight)._

## Research

[PR #7145](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7145) moved the coordinator actor and worker actor into flat `coordinator.py` and `worker.py` modules. The current `execution.py` is 726 lines: `ZephyrContext` occupies lines 228–704, lines 73–225 define its execution IDs, retry classification, resource packing, lifecycle enums, and owned-pool state, and `_print_plan` at lines 706–726 is called only by `ZephyrContext`. Removing the context therefore leaves no independently owned implementation; the other names exposed through the module are imported dependencies or accidental re-exports.

There are 85 repository files with `from zephyr.execution import ...`; 82 import `ZephyrContext`, while a few obtain `ZephyrExecutionResult` or `ZephyrWorkerError` from the wrong defining module. Draft [PR #7948](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7948) also edits `execution.py` for stage checkpoints, so it will have a delete/modify or rename conflict and must transplant those edits into `context.py` if this refactor lands first. It does not duplicate this refactor.

Relevant code:

- [`execution.py#L73-L225`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a109388d188bc177ce7ed80fe9da09e66acdc02/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L73-L225) — context-only helpers and pool state
- [`execution.py#L228-L704`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a109388d188bc177ce7ed80fe9da09e66acdc02/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L228-L704) — `ZephyrContext`
- [`execution.py#L706-L726`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a109388d188bc177ce7ed80fe9da09e66acdc02/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/execution.py#L706-L726) — context-only plan rendering
- [`coordinator.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a109388d188bc177ce7ed80fe9da09e66acdc02/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/coordinator.py#L1) — coordinator-owned execution state
- [`worker.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9a109388d188bc177ce7ed80fe9da09e66acdc02/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/worker.py#L1) — worker-owned execution state

## Proposed fix

Move `execution.py` in full to `context.py` and delete `execution.py`. The resulting flat layout matches `coordinator.py` and `worker.py` and uses the fewest files:

```text
zephyr/
  context.py       # ZephyrContext and its pool/lifecycle implementation
  coordinator.py   # coordinator actor and pipeline state
  worker.py        # worker actor and task threads
  stage_io.py      # task/runner protocols and worker errors
```

`context.py` remains about 726 lines because its supporting enums, pool type, resource validation, retry classification, plan output, and lifecycle helpers have one coherent owner: `ZephyrContext`. Splitting those single-consumer internals again would add module coupling without creating a reusable boundary or reducing a cycle. `MAX_IRIS_WORKER_REPLICAS` stays in `context.py` because it defines the context's pool-cap policy; `_require_resolvable_worker_handles` also stays private there, regardless of its direct test import.

The dependency invariant is `context.py` → `coordinator.py`, `worker.py`, and `stage_io.py`. Those leaf modules must not import `context.py`.

Repository imports move atomically to their defining modules:

- `ZephyrContext`, `MAX_IRIS_WORKER_REPLICAS` → `zephyr.context`
- `ZephyrExecutionResult` → `zephyr.coordinator`
- `ZephyrWorkerError` → `zephyr.stage_io`
- private context tests → `zephyr.context`

No `zephyr.execution` or package-root re-export remains. This preserves behavior and signatures but intentionally breaks the old module import path, consistent with the repository's no-backward-compatibility policy and `zephyr/__init__.py` guidance against re-export hubs. All in-repository consumers will migrate in the same change. An exhaustive search across Python, docs, examples, and package guidance must find zero `zephyr.execution` references afterward. The three `dataset.py` examples that currently import nonexistent `zephyr.execution.load_jsonl` will be corrected to `zephyr.readers`; this is required to eliminate the old module path, not unrelated cleanup. `test_execution.py` keeps its name because it is a behavioral suite spanning context, coordinator, worker, and stage I/O.

### Costs and risks

- About 85 import sites change mechanically, increasing rebase conflicts despite no runtime behavior change.
- Out-of-repository callers using `zephyr.execution` must update their imports.
- PR #7948 must move its checkpoint-related context edits during rebase.

### Rejected alternatives

- Keep `execution.py` as a compatibility shim: conflicts with repository policy and preserves an ambiguous import surface.
- Leave constants or aliases in `execution.py`: the residual file would have no coherent owner.
- Restore the earlier `execution/` package proposal from [PR #5910](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5910): PR #7145 already established the flatter, lower-file-count layout requested in this issue.

### Testing

No new import-existence test: collection, type checking, and the zero-reference search cover relocation without pinning an implementation detail. Run the context/execution, memory-store, runner, and dataset tests for fast feedback; then the full safe Zephyr suite, `uv run pyrefly`, and `./infra/pre-commit.py --all-files --fix`.

### Open question

- Are there known out-of-repository consumers that need coordinated notice before the module-path change? None are visible from this repository, so the implementation will proceed without a shim.

issues.body: It's using a weird structure today. At the very least we should use msgpack to encode a defined class, better yet, we could check out msgspec or just use a protobuf.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS.md, fix-issue, and author-pr skills
- [x] Locate relevant code in `lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py`
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight against open PRs
- [x] Post research + recommendation (no PR opened due to overlap)

**Research**

The sidecar today is encoded as a raw `dict` via `msgspec.msgpack.Encoder()` and parsed back into a raw dict with manual `.get()` / `ValueError` checks. Schema: `shards: dict[str, list[tuple[int, int]]]`, `max_chunk_rows: dict[str, int]`, `avg_item_bytes: float`. Switching to a `msgspec.Struct` defines the schema, drops the validation boilerplate in `_read_sidecar_slice`, and lets `msgspec.msgpack.Decoder(SidecarMeta)` enforce types at decode time. ~50-line change confined to the helpers.

Relevant code:
- [`shuffle.py#L145-L172`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py#L145-L172) — encoder/decoder/write helpers
- [`shuffle.py#L192-L224`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py#L192-L224) — `_read_sidecar_slice` with `.get()` / `ValueError` validation
- [`shuffle.py#L645-L653`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/shuffle.py#L645-L653) — sidecar dict constructed in `ScatterWriter.close()`

**Overlap — not opening a PR**

PR #5963 (`[zephyr] Move scatter internals to Polars & Parquet`, same author) rewrites `shuffle.py` end-to-end, including sidecar contents: `max_chunk_rows` is removed, byte ranges become `{paths, bytes}` lists, and `_write_scatter_meta` / `_read_sidecar_slice` / `ScatterWriter.close()` are all touched. A typed-sidecar PR on `main` would conflict with every site PR 5963 modifies, and the post-#5963 schema is what should actually be typed.

**Proposed Fix**

Define the Struct against the post-#5963 schema and land it either as a commit on that PR or as a follow-up after it merges:

```python
class SidecarShard(msgspec.Struct):
    paths: list[str]
    bytes: list[int]

class SidecarMeta(msgspec.Struct):
    shards: dict[str, SidecarShard]
    avg_item_bytes: float = 0.0

_SIDECAR_DECODER = msgspec.msgpack.Decoder(SidecarMeta)
```

`_read_sidecar_slice` then becomes typed field access (no `.get()`, no manual `ValueError` raises — `msgspec` raises on decode for missing/wrong-type fields), and `ScatterWriter.close()` constructs a `SidecarMeta` directly instead of a dict literal. Deferring implementation pending PR #5963.

`infra/pulumi/README.md`'s Future Work already flags this: no schema or component exists for object storage; buckets are created by hand, lifecycle rules are applied by the imperative `infra/configure_buckets.py` (GCS/R2/CoreWeave object storage, TTL rules only, never creates buckets), and it's undecided whether Pulumi should provision a bucket per cluster or keep the current mix of per-cluster buckets and shared cross-region reuse.

Bucket-scoped IAM access is currently ad hoc and inconsistent: `infra/probes` scopes `roles/storage.objectUser` to one bucket and object-name prefix via an IAM condition, while `infra/evaldash` grants `roles/storage.objectViewer` project-wide (a comment in `infra/evaldash/__main__.py` already flags this as broader than necessary). Design this together with bucket provisioning and lifecycle rules so a service's storage access is declared alongside its other grants — e.g. "gets Iris access and read access to bucket X" as one reviewable unit — rather than each project inventing its own scope. Depends on deciding the per-cluster-vs-shared-bucket question and likely follows the IAM-import work in #7576.

- [`buckets/gcp.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7940e3f1aad75121155026b1aaa33f83c06d7c69/infra/pulumi/src/iac/buckets/gcp.py#L33-L77) - shared GCS bucket ownership in #8343
- [`iam.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/662b4bc1b7b548249e432ce709fb09576d240f05/infra/pulumi/src/iac/gcp/iam.py#L326-L347) - existing non-authoritative bucket grants
- [`iam_data.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/662b4bc1b7b548249e432ce709fb09576d240f05/infra/pulumi/src/iac/gcp/iam_data.yaml#L1341-L1382) - project-wide storage roles
- [`evaldash/__main__.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/662b4bc1b7b548249e432ce709fb09576d240f05/infra/evaldash/__main__.py#L83-L89) - overbroad evaldash grant
- [`probes/deploy.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/662b4bc1b7b548249e432ce709fb09576d240f05/infra/probes/deploy/deploy.py#L202-L232) - imperative probe grants

# Service-oriented storage access

Keep the current shared bucket topology. GCS has one data bucket per serving region, CoreWeave has one per CoreWeave object-storage region, and R2 supplies the shared North America fallback. Cluster-specific buckets would duplicate data already routed by `config/marin.yaml` and `config/coreweave.yaml` and would require a migration policy for shared datasets. PR #8343 should remain the bucket and lifecycle implementation; this change supplies its missing access model.

## Challenges

The imported IAM schema is organized by GCP resource, which is useful for auditing a bucket but scatters one service account across project roles, secrets, repositories, and buckets. Application stacks also create some of the same physical IAM members, so adding a bucket argument to each project would retain split ownership. GCS supports non-authoritative bucket IAM members and CEL prefix conditions; CoreWeave and R2 currently authenticate through externally provisioned S3 credentials whose secret values cannot enter Pulumi state.

## Costs / Risks

- Moving checked-in grants into service-oriented records changes the IAM schema and writer, although provider IDs and Pulumi resource names can remain unchanged.
- Narrowing evaldash from project-wide access needs a staged apply so the bucket grant exists before the broad grant is removed.
- CoreWeave and R2 bucket creation remains declarative, but data-plane credential creation and rotation remain external until they can be represented without secret material in Pulumi state.

## Design

Add a `service_access` section to `infra/pulumi/src/iac/gcp/iam_data.yaml`. Each entry names one service-account member and groups its project roles, secret access, Artifact Registry access, and GCS bucket access. Bucket entries require a role and bucket; an optional `object_prefix` lowers to a canonical `resource.name.startsWith(...)` condition. The loader rejects an IAM tuple declared both under `service_access` and the resource-oriented inventory.

```yaml
service_access:
- name: infra-probes
  member: serviceAccount:infra-probes@hai-gcp-models.iam.gserviceaccount.com
  project_roles: [roles/logging.logWriter]
  artifact_repositories:
  - { location: us-central1, repository: marin, role: roles/artifactregistry.reader }
  buckets:
  - bucket: marin-us-central1
    role: roles/storage.objectUser
    object_prefix: infra/probes/
- name: marin-evaldash
  member: serviceAccount:marin-evaldash@hai-gcp-models.iam.gserviceaccount.com
  project_roles: [roles/cloudsql.client, roles/compute.viewer]
  secrets: [cloudsql-evals-password, cw-object-storage-key-id, cw-object-storage-key-secret]
  buckets:
  - { bucket: marin-eval-metadata, role: roles/storage.objectViewer }
```

The parser lowers these records into the existing `GcpRoleGrant`, `GcpSecretIam`, `GcpBucketIam`, and `GcpArtifactRepositoryIam` collections before `GcpIam` declares resources. Existing logical names and import IDs stay stable. Moving the already-imported probe, evaldash, secret, and repository grants changes the source layout without changing state identities.

Migrate the two concrete cases. Remove the `gcloud ... add-iam-policy-binding` calls from the probe `create` path and declare its prefix grant in `service_access`. Remove `roles/storage.objectViewer` from evaldash's Cloud Run project roles, delete that member from the project-wide imported grant, and add bucket-scoped viewer access to `marin-eval-metadata`. Iris `allowed_submitters` remains in the cluster configs; an onboarding PR can change those runtime authorization lists and the service record together without making Iris depend on the infrastructure package.

Apply the GCS transition in two operations after merge: target/import the probe bucket member and create the evaldash bucket member, then run the full `marin` update that removes evaldash's project-wide viewer. The normal program remains non-authoritative throughout. PR #8343 and this IAM change can merge independently because both target existing bucket names.

## Testing

Parser tests cover service-record lowering, canonical prefix expressions, duplicate tuple rejection, and checked-in YAML round-tripping. Pulumi resource tests verify the lowered records retain the existing provider IDs and use `gcp.storage.BucketIAMMember`. The deployment check is a `marin` preview with no bucket replacement or deletion; the staged IAM apply must show only the expected member import/create before the final project-member deletion.

## Open Questions

- Should a follow-up manage CoreWeave bucket policies once service identities exist independently of the S3 secret values? The first change leaves current external keys unchanged.
- Should all machine principals move into `service_access`, or should the first migration stay limited to evaldash and probes until the schema has survived one apply?

comments.body:
🤖 #8363 overshot the issue. The existing GCP IAM model already supports the minimal change; it does not need `service_access`, a schema-version bump, or a transfer of all probe IAM ownership.

1. CoreWeave and R2 access

CoreWeave authorization can be managed with Pulumi. The official provider exposes [`ObjectStorageBucketPolicy`](https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/coreweave/api-docs/objectstoragebucketpolicy/) and [`ObjectStorageOrganizationAccessPolicy`](https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/coreweave/api-docs/objectstorageorganizationaccesspolicy/), which bind S3 or `cwobject` actions to CoreWeave, SAML, or OIDC principals. The provider does not expose an access-key resource. [CoreWeave's control-plane API](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/storage/object-storage/reference/object-storage-api-ref) can issue and revoke keys, and its [current guidance](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/storage/object-storage/auth-access/about) recommends workload identity federation for production credentials. For Marin's human-issued/shared static keys, Pulumi could manage a policy for the key owner's principal, but that would describe a person's access instead of a service identity. I would leave key issuance outside Pulumi and treat WIF plus Pulumi-managed policies as separate follow-up work.

R2 access is technically manageable through Pulumi's [`cloudflare.AccountToken`](https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/cloudflare/api-docs/accounttoken/) or `ApiToken` resources. [Cloudflare supports Object Read or Object Read & Write tokens scoped to named buckets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/tokens/). The token ID is the S3 access-key ID, and the S3 secret is derived from the token value. Creating one with Pulumi therefore puts a credential output in Pulumi state and requires a bootstrap credential with `Account API Tokens Write`. #8343 deliberately keeps provider credentials outside Pulumi configuration and state. I would keep R2 token ownership out of #7580 and open a separate design if we want Pulumi to own credential creation, rotation, storage, and distribution.

2. Minimal GCS change

Current `main` already has `GcpBucketIam`, condition parsing, `gcp.storage.BucketIAMMember`, and Program-first imports. Append the two issue-specific grants under the existing `buckets:` key in `iam_data.yaml`:

```yaml
buckets:
- bucket: marin-eval-metadata
  grants:
  - role: roles/storage.objectViewer
    members:
    - serviceAccount:marin-evaldash@hai-gcp-models.iam.gserviceaccount.com
- bucket: marin-us-central1
  grants:
  - role: roles/storage.objectUser
    members:
    - serviceAccount:infra-probes@hai-gcp-models.iam.gserviceaccount.com
    condition:
      title: infra-probes-prefix
      expression: resource.name.startsWith("projects/_/buckets/marin-us-central1/objects/infra/probes/")
      description: Limit infra-probes SA object access to its rollup prefix
```

Then remove the evaldash project-wide viewer from both `iam_data.yaml` and `infra/evaldash/__main__.py`, and remove only the bucket IAM mutation from `infra/probes/deploy/deploy.py`. Leave probe service-account creation, Artifact Registry access, and logging access where they are; those are outside this issue's bucket-access scope. Import the existing probe bucket binding and apply the bucket grants before removing evaldash's broad grant.

I recommend rewriting #8363 to that scope on current `main`. The result should be a small YAML migration plus two ad-hoc call-site removals, using the IAM machinery already merged in #7576.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Generic domain routing with compact conditional references outperformed the original hardcoded layout without weakening mutation safety. PR #8636 consolidates Iris and Finelog guidance and removes six top-level skills.

## Description

The experiment compared the original skill set, generic-only and layered variants, and a final consolidated layout. Fresh Luna/medium sessions answered identical Iris job, federation, telemetry, monitoring, deployment, accelerator, and Kubernetes recovery questions. Separate Luna sessions graded anonymous answers against fixed correctness, provenance, safety, and completion rubrics. No live infrastructure mutations were allowed.

Prior work: [the agent docs retrospective](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4481#issuecomment-4196059208) reported reliable routing for narrow task titles. This experiment tested whether progressive disclosure could retain those workflows beneath broader domain entry points.

## Hypothesis or Goal

A concise Iris navigator and generic Finelog query skill should improve cross-cutting diagnosis. Compact references should replace narrow workflow skills only if their authorization and recovery contracts remain discoverable.

## Status

Complete. The selected implementation is in #8636.

## Links

* Pull request: #8636
* [Logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/iris-skill-generalization/.agents/logbooks/iris-skill-generalization.md)
* [Benchmark and rubric](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/iris-skill-generalization/.agents/projects/iris_skill_generalization/benchmark.md)
* [Max-RSS example](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/230)
* W&B Report: not applicable

## Decision Log

* 2026-08-24: Current, generic-only, and layered layouts scored 75/80, 79/80, and 79/80.
* 2026-08-24: The refined generic layout scored 99/100 versus 94/100 on a fresh replication, including 20/20 on held-out telemetry-temporality and federation-route cases.
* 2026-08-24: The final two-entry-point layout scored 46/50 versus 42/50 for the original hardcoded layout on monitoring, rollout, accelerator, stuck-pod, and max-RSS cases.
* 2026-08-24: A focused forward-test confirmed the corrected dirty-tree rollout command remained discoverable.

## Conclusion

Use `use-iris` and `query-finelog` as the domain entry points. Keep job monitoring, controller rollout, dev accelerator, and stuck-pod contracts as short references loaded only when needed. Keep distinct top-level skills for cross-domain or production-specific triggers such as Zephyr babysitting, hero runs, profiling, and debugging.

The evaluation used one answer per layout, so its scores establish directional evidence rather than statistical confidence. The candidate nevertheless won all three comparisons, generalized to held-out cases, selected every consolidated reference, and had no mutation-safety deduction.

comments.body:
# Job Summary: d=2560 MoE on 10T tokens

Big-batch d=2560 MoE training run on ~10T tokens (~1.2e23 FLOPs), with the May Recipe baked in. Below are sections on model, optimizer, training, scaling principles, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters

- **hidden_dim**: 2560
- **num_layers**: 26 (heuristic-derived: `round(2560 / (64 + 4·log2(2560) − 9))`)
- **num_heads**: 20 (`hidden_dim / 128`)
- **num_kv_heads**: 5 (GQA 4:1; largest divisor of 20 ≤ 5)
- **head_dim**: 128
- **intermediate_dim**: 1280 (`ceil(d/2/128)·128`)
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim**: 2560 (= d)
- **num_experts**: 256
- **num_experts_per_token**: 4
- **vocab_size**: 128,256
- **max_seq_len**: 4096
- **sliding_window**: 4096
- **active_params**: 2.34B (2.01B core + 0.33B lm_head; excludes embed per guidelines)
- **total_params**: 67.1B (66.4B core + 0.33B embed + 0.33B lm_head)

### Features

- **GQA**: 4:1 ratio (20 Q heads, 5 KV heads).
- **QB Routing**: stop-gradient bias updated each step from previous step's QB-β statistics (applied inside JIT).
- **Sigmoid Combine Weights**: sigmoid on unbiased router logits for selected experts.
- **GatedNorm**: rank-128 low-rank gating after RMSNorm, pre-attention and pre-MLP.
- **XSA**: subtracts V-parallel component from attention output per head.
- **Attention Gate**: learned per-head sigmoid gate on attention output, initialized to zero.
- **Shared Expert**: dense FFN (d=2560) in parallel with routed experts per layer.
- **Sliding Window**: every 4th layer (plus last) uses full window (4096); others use half (2048).
- **Half-RoPE on every layer**: RoPE applied only to the first half of Q/K per head (`q[..., :head_dim/2]`, `k[..., :head_dim/2]`). The second half is rope-free on every layer.
- **PKO (Partial Key Offset)**: on every-4th + last layer (7 of 26 layers here), the rope-free second half of K is additionally shifted by 1 position with doc-start zeroing.
- **QK Gain**: `qk_mult = 1.3`.
- **Split w_gate / w_up**: separate weight matrices for SwiGLU gate and up projections (`split_w_gate_up=True`).
- **Routing renorm sum**: 2.5 (combined-feature baseline).
- **Router z-loss**: disabled (`router_z_loss_coef = 0`).
- **Expert dispatch**: ring (May Recipe default; `moe_implementation` not exposed in current model config).

## 2. Optimizer

### Hyperparameters

(Using the refit `MoeAdamHHeuristic` from #5951.)

- **adam_lr**: 0.000432  (= `0.06602 · 1e13^-0.395 · 2560^-0.150 · √(2048·4096)`)
- **muonh_lr (= adamh_lr)**: 0.001870  (= adam_lr · 13/3)
- **beta1**: 0.9062
- **beta2**: 0.95 (clamped; `0.999^(2048/32) = 0.938` → clipped up to 0.95)
- **epsilon**: 1.06e−14  (= `1e-15 · √((32·1e13)/(2048·1.4e9))`)
- **weight_decay**: 0
- **max_grad_norm**: None (1pct-noclip schedule)
- **warmup**: 1% (= 11,921 steps)
- **decay**: None (linear schedule decays to 0 over full run)
- **min_lr_ratio**: 0.0
- **lr_schedule**: linear
- **z_loss_weight**: 0.0

### Features

- **MuonH** (`GrugMoeMuonHConfig`): scale-invariant Newton-Schulz updates on the `muonh` group (matmuls + GatedNorms), Frobenius hyperball step on top. Used in place of AdamH on weight matrices.
- **Multi-group optimizer**: 3 groups —
  - `muonh`: attn matmuls, MoE expert matmuls (gate/up/down), shared expert, GatedNorms.
  - `adamh`: lm_head / output_proj (LR = `muonh_lr`).
  - `adam`: token_embed, router weight + bias, attn_gate, 1-D norm weights (LR = `adam_lr`).

## 3. Training

- **hardware**: v4-1024 us-central2 (= 512 chips).
- **num_train_steps**: 1,192,093  (= `1e13 / (2048 · 4096)`)
- **batch_size**: 2,048 sequences
- **seq_len**: 4,096
- **tokens_per_batch**: 8.39M (= `2048 · 4096`)
- **total_tokens**: 1.00e13 (= 10T)
- **compute_budget**: ~1.21e23 FLOPs (= `6 · 2.01e9 · 1e13`)
- **mixed_precision**: `params=float32, compute=bfloat16, output=bfloat16`
- **expert_parallelism**: 4
- **data**: Nemotron mix (block-shuffled) with default validation sets
- **checkpoints**: every 10 minutes (rolling temporary), permanent every 5,000 steps

## 4. Scaling Principles

All optimizer hyperparameters derived from the refit MuonH May Recipe heuristic (issue #5951, R² = 0.996 on 17 cells).

### Learning rates (current heuristic)

- **adam_lr** = `0.06602 · tokens^-0.395 · dim^-0.150 · √(B·seq_len)`, capped at 0.05.
- **muonh_lr** = `(13/3) · adam_lr`.

### Momentum and precision

- **beta1** = 0.9062 (fixed)
- **beta2** = `clip(0.999^(B/32), 0.95, 0.9999)` → 0.95 at B=2048
- **epsilon** = `1e-15 · √((32·T) / (B·1.4e9))`

### Architecture scaling

- **num_layers** = `round(hidden_dim / (64 + 4·log2(hidden_dim) − 9))` → 26 for d=2560
- **num_heads** = `hidden_dim / 128`
- **num_kv_heads** = 4:1 GQA, largest divisor of num_heads ≤ num_heads/4
- **intermediate_dim** = `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) · 128`
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim** = hidden_dim
- **initializer_std** = `0.5 / sqrt(hidden_dim)` ≈ 0.00988
- **num_experts** = 256, **num_experts_per_token** = 4 (fixed for May Recipe; differs from the 64-expert v16 baseline used in the 1e23 summary)

### Schedule

- **warmup** = 1% of training (1pct-noclip baseline)
- **decay** = linear all the way to 0 (no separate decay phase)
- **max_grad_norm** = None (no clipping)

## 5. Outputs

- **GCS checkpoint path**: `gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_may_d2560_10T/marin-big-run-moe_may_d2560_10T-XXXXXX/checkpoints` (pending — actual hash assigned at submission)
- **WandB run link**: `https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/marin-big-run-moe_may_d2560_10T` (pending)
- **Final eval metrics**: pending (run not submitted yet)
  - eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb
  - eval/paloma/macro_loss
  - eval/uncheatable_eval/macro_loss
- **Throughput** (mean over last 100 logged steps): pending

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: David's idea to use Replica sharding brings it down from 55 days to 45 days. All v4-2048 runs require 2x batch size to get good MFU, up from 33 million to 67 million. However on further testing, 67 million batch size is not training stably, compared to 33 million batch size. https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Batch-Size-Testing-67B-A2B-MoE-on-10T-tokens--VmlldzoxNzM1MTA2OQ As is standard, we scale learning rate with batch_size^0.5. This assumes that you get a less noisy gradient estimate as you scale up batch size, which typically occurs up until the critical batch size, at which point there are diminishing gains. In a prior [Issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4432) I estimated the critical batch size for compute optimal runs on our prior (similar) architecture. At compute optimal, the critical batch size is much smaller for our model size, estimated to be roughly 6-10M tokens, after which we get reduced performance. However since we are heavily overtraining, a larger batch size can be justified, since when we get to lower loss regime a larger batch size will be helpful. Many works calculate critical batch size as a function of the token budget. 22.91 · T^0.47 for 10 trillion tokens gives 29.5 million tokens, fit on AdamW. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.13738. Indications here that critical batch size is higher for Muon compared to Adam: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/1565. Llama 3 report: 3.4.1 Initial Pre-Training We pre-train Llama 3 405B using AdamW with a peak learning rate of 8 × 10−5, a linear warm up of 8,000 steps, and a cosine learning rate schedule decaying to 8 × 10−7 over 1,200,000 steps. We use a lower batch size early in training to improve training stability, and increase it subsequently to improve efficiency. Specifically, we use an initial batch size of 4M tokens and sequences of length 4,096, and double these values to a batch size of 8M sequences of 8,192 tokens after pre-training 252M tokens. We double the batch size again to 16M after pre-training on 2.87T tokens. We found this training recipe to be very stable: we observed few loss spikes and did not require interventions to correct for model training divergence. The key line here is "We use a lower batch size early in training to improve training stability". Training run references: -Arcee trained Trinity nano and mini on 10T tokens pretrain, with batch size 16 million. Then doubled to 32 million midway. -Nemotron 3 Super used 25 million batch size on 25T tokens. Given our atypical hardware setup (1024 tpu chips on a v4-2048) and smaller model size (2B active), batch size is a very high priority axis for achieving MFU, so we want to push batch size as high as possible. (of course there is some theoretical limit where we shift from diminishing gains to near zero gains). It is plausible that we could achieve a stable run start by increasing the warmup percentage from 1pct to 10pct. However, given the literature above, and the fact that we already have evidence that 33 million batch size can perform a stable warmup, it seems more sensible to start the run at 33 million at reduced MFU. If we were to keep the run at 33 million tokens per batch for the full run, we will get 63 days to complete. If we did the full run at 67 million tokens per batch, we will get 45 days to complete. Depending on if/when we shift the batch size, will determine where between 63 days and 45 days the run falls.

Plan:
Start the run on the full v4-2048 at batch size 33 million so we can achieve a stable warmup. Then, discuss with team on timing tradeoffs.

comments.body: (This dynamic is how understood but leaving this comment for historical accuracy) Not yet understood dynamic where numerical stability seems to suffer at full node count. Here we do a test on a very small d512 model for 200 steps (with an extremely agressive batch size). On v5p-8 it trains as expected. On v4-2048 it diverges with EP=2, or replica in (2, 16, 1024). If I move to full fp32 on output and compute, as opposed to bfloat16, it not longer diverges, but still performs substantially worse than vp5-8. This confirms that we see numerical gaps, even at fp32. Here we can see that the 33 million tokens per batch on v4-2048 is training stably, but its loss curve is a bit worse than we were getting on v4-1024. The only hardware dependent calc outside numerical precision I am aware of is the local sorting for QB. The difference in trajectory is visible in the first 10 steps, where QB has no impact. This was validated by running a full global sort version of QB and seeing it still follow the v4-2048 trajectory.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: The root cause of the issue is that the sharded NS calc in Muon was silently dropping when num_matrices didn't evenly divide into num_chips. This was originally written on v4-1024 where 256*26 is divisible by 512 chips. However it isn't divisible by 1024 chips. The fix was to explicitly replicate the NS calc over the same size as the replica axis, and also patch the silent failure. After doing this, we get stable replication of the v5p-8 d512 200 step run: Increasing precision to fp32 was helping the non orthogonalized approach not diverge, but not addressing the root cause. Lack of orthogonalization explains why the loss curve started better and then got worse over time, similar to how adam can beat muon in first couple steps. Given this knowledge, it is likely that the instability at 67 million token batch size is only due to failing to orthogonalize the gradient. So, we likely could do the full run at 67 million token batch size. However, starting at 33 million batch size for the first 5% of the run will likely be more token efficient, and only add 1 day of runtime. (46 day total). This also lets us validate the full warmup curve against the v4-1024 warmup curve which ran at 33 million batch size. Reflecting on the bug: 1. Transitioning from small scale tests to prod scale implementation will always require iterating on the code. (lax.scan to fit in memory, iterating on the sharding implementation). 2. This introduces risk of incorrect implementation. In particular due to perception of time pressure of having the hardware sit idle. 3. This incorrectness can be subtely incorrect in ML world. (though in this particular case this issue should have errored loudly, but I did not review this agent written resharding close enough) For future runs, recommend we have: 1. Small scale code should have prior code review and be checked into main. 2. After we get large scale code implemented, we should raise PR and get human review on the (ideally minor) changes to get small scale code working at prod scale. 3. Always replicate a small scale run on the prod hardware. (this has now been done for this run) 4. Have a script that runs series of validation checks against the first 200 steps of wandb logs. (checking all param inits, param norms over initial training with hyperball, routing entropy, activity across all layers, train stability, etc). These always get eye-balled but the level of rigor is not the same.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Preregistered loss target for stage 1 of the run (first 8T tokens): 2.269 paloma macro loss when evaled at seqlen 8192 on 1024 sequences per eval. This projection is viewed as our best estimate, but there are a large number of assumptions underpinning it: 1. Assuming an irreducible loss of 1.4. Prior large scale runs at seqlen 4k have indicated an irreducible loss of 1.5. Extending the seqlen to 8k should slightly reduce this, by reducing the number of evals that start a sequence mid-context. 2. The smaller scale runs had no logit z loss. After observing large grad norm on the d1024 run, I did a follow up experiment re-adding z loss to the final logit, which helped control the gradient and gave better evals and train loss. https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Z-Loss-Under-OverTrain-650B-tokens---VmlldzoxNzMyODk1NQ. 3. We are heavily increasing the batch size for the 10T run, which will increase the final loss. I am assuming that point 2 will roughly cancel out with this. 4. We are extrapolating from 3 points- our prior 1e23 run extrapolated at compute optimal from over 20 points. In particular, runs at d512 seem to extrapolate worse due to heavier parameter skew in lm_head due to high vocab size of 128k. We chose to not extrapolate from more points to enable the 10T run to start sooner. 5. We will be at 24% peak LR at the end of stage 1. Predicting model performance before full LR cooldown may have different dynamics as we scale. Given these assumptions, I anticipate we will be able to use the actual achieved loss to update our knowledge of training dynamics and which assumptions to revisit.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Job summary for the d=2560 67B / 2B-active MoE 10T pretrain

# Job Summary: 67B / 2B-active MoE 10T pretrain (d=2560, MuonH, v4-2048)

~10.07T-token MuonH MoE pretrain at d=2560 / 67B total params / 2.01B active per token (run_id `moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep16_bs4096_seq8192_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_10T`; batch ramp from 4,096 → 8,192 at step 15,000, with total steps reduced so total tokens stay near 10T). Below are sections on model, optimizer, training, and scaling principles.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters

- **hidden_dim**: 2560
- **num_layers**: 26
- **num_heads**: 20
- **num_kv_heads**: 5 (GQA 4:1)
- **head_dim**: 128
- **intermediate_dim**: 1280 (MoE expert FFN; `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) * 128`)
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim**: 2560 (= hidden_dim)
- **num_experts**: 256
- **num_experts_per_token**: 4
- **vocab_size**: 128,256
- **max_seq_len**: 8,192
- **sliding_window**: 2,048
- **total_params**: 67.1B
- **active_params**: 2.01B per token (2.34B w/ lm_head)

### Features

- **GQA**: 4:1 ratio (20 Q heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128)
- **QB Routing**: stop-gradient bias updated each step from previous step's QB-β statistics (applied inside JIT)
- **Sigmoid Combine Weights**: sigmoid on unbiased router logits for the K=4 selected experts (not softmax). Combine weights are then renormalized to sum to **2.5** across the K selected experts (`_ROUTING_RENORM_SUM = 2.5` in `model.py:51`), which effectively rescales the routed-expert contribution per token by 2.5× compared to a standard sum-to-1 (softmax-style) normalization.
- **GatedNorm**: rank-128 low-rank gating after RMSNorm, pre-attention and pre-MLP
- **Shared Expert**: dense FFN (d=2560) in parallel with routed experts per layer
- **Sliding Window**: every 4th layer + final layer uses full window (8,192); the other 19 layers use the short window (2,048). Layout: 7 long / 19 short (`i % 4 == 3 or i == num_layers - 1`).
- **disable_long_rope**: long (full-attention) layers skip rotary embedding entirely. Short (windowed) layers still apply half-RoPE.
- **disable_pko**: no per-key offset on long layers. Plain attention only.
- **RoPE**: partial rotary — only half of `head_dim` is rotated (the leading 64 of 128 dims), the rest is passed through unchanged. Applied on short (windowed) layers only; long (full-attention) layers skip RoPE entirely per `disable_long_rope`.
- **ArrayStacked + scan**: all 26 blocks stacked via `jax.lax.scan` (`use_array_stacked_blocks=True`) for reduced compile time and HBM footprint

## 2. Optimizer

### Hyperparameters

- **muonh_lr**: 0.003733 → **0.005279** at step 15,000 (×√2 with the BS doubling)
- **adam_lr**: 0.000861 → **0.001218** at step 15,000 (= muonh_lr / (13/3); also ×√2)
- **beta1**: 0.9062 (unchanged across the BS ramp)
- **beta2**: 0.95 — clamped both before and after the ramp (raw formula 0.999^(B*S/131072) gives 0.774 pre-ramp and 0.599 post-ramp; both clamp to 0.95)
- **epsilon**: ~8.01 × 10⁻¹⁹ → **~5.66 × 10⁻¹⁹** at step 15,000 (÷√2 with the BS doubling)
- **weight_decay**: 0
- **max_grad_norm**: None (no clipping in MuonH 1pct-noclip schedule)
- **warmup**: 0.01 (1% of training; ~3,000 steps)
- **decay**: None (linear decay over the whole post-warmup period)
- **min_lr_ratio**: 0.05 (decay to 5% of peak by end-of-training)
- **lr_schedule**: linear
- **z_loss_weight**: 1e-4 (logit z-loss; router z-loss = 0)

### Features

- **MuonH (Muon + Frobenius hyperball)**: Newton-Schulz orthogonalization on weight matrices followed by a scale-invariant Frobenius-hyperball projection. Three LR groups:
  - **muonh** — 2D weight matrices and stacked MoE expert weights (NS + hyperball)
  - **adamh** — `lm_head` / `output_proj`. AdamH = Adam moments + Frobenius hyperball (`scale_by_adamh`); no Newton-Schulz. Uses the same LR schedule as muonh.
  - **adam** — biases, RMSNorm scales, router weights, gated-norm scales, and (via `rmsnorm_to_adam=True`) stacked RMSNorm scales
- **Multi-group optimizer**: separate optax chains per group routed by parameter path (see `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:create_mask`).
- **Logit Z-Loss**: penalizes large output-logit norm to stabilize training (no router z-loss in this run).

## 3. Training

- **hardware**: v4-2048 (1,024 chips), us-central2, production priority, --no-preemptible
- **num_train_steps**: 157,500 (reduced from 300,000 to absorb the batch-size doubling and hold total tokens ~constant)
- **batch_size**: 4,096 → 8,192 sequences (step change at step 15,000 ≈ 5% of training)
- **seq_len**: 8,192
- **tokens_per_step**: 33,554,432 (~33.5M) for steps 0–14,999; 67,108,864 (~67.1M) for steps 15,000–157,499
- **total_tokens**: ~1.007 × 10¹³ (~10.07T) — 5.03 × 10¹¹ from the BS=4,096 phase (15,000 steps) + 9.56 × 10¹² from the BS=8,192 phase (142,500 steps)
- **compute_budget**: ~1.69 × 10²³ FLOPs (SWA-aware, with lm_head)
- **mixed_precision**: `params=float32,compute=bfloat16,output=bfloat16`
- **mesh**: `(replica_dcn=16, data=64, expert=1, model=1)`. EP=1, `replica_axis_size=16`. Batch is sharded across (replica_dcn, data, expert) → 1,024 shards.
- **expert_parallelism**: 1 (no expert sharding; routed experts replicated across the expert axis)
- **data**: datakit MoE mixture (`_datakit_data_config`, simulated epoching disabled) with default paloma validation sets
- **eval cadence**: every 3,000 steps; `eval_batch_size=1024`, `max_eval_batches=1` (8.39M tokens per eval)
- **checkpoints**: permanent every 3,000 steps; temp save every 60 minutes; auto-resume on preemption

## 4. Scaling Principles

All optimizer hyperparameters derived from the MuonH May Recipe refit (issue #5951, 17 finished cells across d ∈ {512, 768, 1024, 1280} × R ∈ {4, 10, 20, 60, 120, 240} × lr_mult ∈ {0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6}, R² = 0.996). Reference seq_len = 4096; conversions assume `tokens_per_batch = batch_size * seq_len`.

### Learning rates

- **muonh_lr** = `18.31 · T^(-0.395) · d^(-0.150) · sqrt(B)`, capped at 0.05
  - Equivalent to `lr_coeff · T^(-0.395) · d^(-0.150) · sqrt(tokens_per_batch)` with `lr_coeff = 0.06602` (= 18.31 / ((13/3) · 64))
  - At T = 1.007e13, d = 2560, B*S = 33.55M → **muonh_lr ≈ 0.003733**
- **adam_lr** = muonh_lr / (13/3) ≈ **0.000861**
- **adamh_lr** = muonh_lr ≈ **0.003733** (the `adamh` group — `lm_head` / `output_proj` — uses the same LR schedule as muonh, via `scale_by_adamh`: Adam moments + Frobenius hyperball, no Newton-Schulz)

### Momentum and precision

- **beta1** = 0.9062 (fixed)
- **beta2** = `clip(0.999^(tokens_per_batch / 131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`
  - At B*S = 33.55M → raw 0.999^256 ≈ 0.774 → clamped to **0.95**
- **epsilon** = `9.676e-18 · sqrt((B0 · T) / (tokens_per_batch · T0))` with B0=32, T0=1.4e9
  - At T = 1.007e13, tokens_per_batch = 33.55M → **epsilon ≈ 8.01e-19**

### Architecture scaling

- **num_layers** = `round(hidden_dim / (64 + 4·log2(hidden_dim) - 9))` = 26 for d=2560
- **num_heads** = `hidden_dim / 128` = 20
- **num_kv_heads** = largest divisor of num_heads ≤ num_heads // 4 = 5 (GQA 4:1)
- **intermediate_dim** = `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) · 128` = 1280
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim** = hidden_dim = 2560
- **initializer_std** ≈ `0.5 / sqrt(2560)` ≈ 0.00988
- **num_experts** = 256, **num_experts_per_token** = 4 (fixed; differs from the 1e23 d=5120 run which used 64 experts)

### Schedule

- **warmup** = 1% of training (~3,000 steps)
- **decay** = none (linear schedule decays over the whole post-warmup period)
- **min_lr_ratio** = 0.05 (decay to 5% of peak)
- **lr_schedule** = linear

## 5. Outputs

- **GCS checkpoint path**: `gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep16_bs4096_seq8192_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_10T-<hash>/checkpoints` (pending — populated on first save)
- **WandB run link**: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep16_bs4096_seq8192_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_10T
- **iris job**: `/larry/iris-run-job-20260627-154212`
- **Final eval metrics** (pending — run in progress):
  - eval/paloma/macro_loss (projected: 2.269 @ 0.8 of training; see issue #6044)
  - eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb
  - eval/uncheatable_eval/macro_loss
- **Throughput** (pending — fill from mean over last 100 logged steps):
  - throughput/mfu
  - throughput/tokens_per_second

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Report where run will be tracked: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/67B-A2B-MoE-on-10T-tokens--VmlldzoxNzM1OTMxMQ

Notable updates to architecture:
1. Since we are planning to extend context out to 262k, there will likely be several iterations on datamix and attention scaling to enable this. To minimize possible confounders during this process, PKO has been disabled, along with RoPE on the global layers. This puts our architecture close to published literature on effective long context extension. Once we have successfully extended context using textbook approaches, then we can consider adding back partial rope and PKO. We may be incurring a 10-20% efficiency hit from this, but the risk/reward tradeoff here of taking a controlled approach seems worthwhile to maximize learnings and our later models.
2. Re-adding final logit z loss. At compute optimal scale, z loss had a neglible impact. However on the new data mix and extreme overtrain, we see meaningful gains from including z loss, both on the train loss and evals. https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Z-Loss-Under-OverTrain-650B-tokens---VmlldzoxNzMyODk1NQ.
3. Batch size schedule. The hardware profile is heavily encouraging us to run at extremely large batch sizes to achieve acceptable MFU. Instead of performing the full run at 67 million tokens per batch, we are running the first 5 pct at half that. Which is the window when smaller batch sizes have the biggest impact.
4. LR decay to 0.05 instead of 0. This is because we will extend out from 64k->262k, and do subsequent posttrain. decay to zero is only optimal if we have no subsequent weight updates.

comments.body:
🤖 **Final 1 T-token cooldown submitted** (third and last in the 67B-a2b 10T campaign)

- **Iris job**: `/larry/iris-run-job-20260815-212009` · [dashboard](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Flarry%2Firis-run-job-20260815-212009)
- **Launcher**: [`experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_cooldown_step141k_seq64k_bs1024_rep8_muon_10T.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b054d8912d/experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_cooldown_step141k_seq64k_bs1024_rep8_muon_10T.py) on branch `june_tpu_67b_a2b`, pinned at commit [`b054d8912d`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/b054d8912d)
- **Reads from**: `gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs8192_seq8192_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_resume15k_v2_10T-9fcc1f/checkpoints/step-141000/` (main-run pretraining checkpoint at 9 T tokens seen; manifest written 2026-08-15 21:16 UTC, complete)
- **Wandb run**: `moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step141k` (fresh — same group `june-tpu-67b-a2b-cooldown` as the two earlier cooldowns)

### Config

| Knob | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resume step | 141,000 | main run's ~9 T-token mark (89.5% of the 157,500-step horizon) |
| Cooldown steps | 15,000 | 1.007 T tokens = ~last 1 T of the 10 T campaign |
| `seq_len` / `batch_size` | 65,536 / 1,024 | 67.1 M tokens/step (unchanged from source's 8,192 × 8,192) |
| `qk_mult` | 1.57 | matches the winning all-layers YaRN `mscale(coef=0.1)` from the step-102k cooldown |
| LR | 0.000822 → 0.000264, linear | joins source at step-141k, decays to source floor over 15k steps |
| Data mix | phase-1 (mix 2) only | main run's been in mix 2 since step 127,500 |
| `resume_data_offset` | **13,824,000** samples | new field: exact-position continuation — see below |
| `hybrid_attention_flops_accounting` | True | 7 full + 19 sw=2048 layers → MFU reports ~0.44× the naive count (honest) |
| Save + eval | every 1,500 steps | 10 permanent saves + 10 evals over the cooldown |
| Iris retries | `--max-retries 100` | auto-recovery on the recurring coord-service TCP-close failure (#7430) |

### Data-position continuation (new mechanism)

Prior cooldowns (step-39k, step-102k) used a fresh mix-2 shuffle from position 0. This one continues main run's mix-2 stream *exactly*:

- Main run consumed **905.97 B mix-2 tokens** between steps 127,500 → 141,000 (13,500 steps × 8,192 seq × 8,192 BS).
- Cooldown at seq=65,536 wants to start at the same underlying token offset → sample-index **13,824,000**.
- New `resume_data_offset` field on `GrugMoeLaunchConfig2xBS` builds a 3-stage BatchSchedule `[(0, 98), (135000, 99), (141000, 1024)]` that lands `cumulative_size(141000)` at exactly 13,824,000 samples. Zero re-consumption of main run's exposure, zero skip past it.
- Per-bucket read positions in each of the 168 mix-2 buckets exactly continue where main run left off; the mixture-shuffle order differs (unavoidable: mixture-shuffle indexes are in cooldown's seq_len enumeration, which is 8× the main run's).
- 12 small-weight buckets will epoch during the 1 T cooldown budget (aggregate ~1.3% extra re-exposure; largest is `c34q4` at 2.88×).

### MFU accounting

Restored the hybrid-attention FLOPs accounting from the step-39k cooldown (originally commit 5681efbe3f, reverted for hash-continuity at the time). At seq=65,536, `lm_flops_per_token` for our 26-layer model (7 full + 19 sliding-window at sw=2048) is **9.74×10⁹** vs. the naive all-full-attention 2.22×10¹⁰ — so `throughput/mfu` will report about 2.28× lower than a naive counter for the same wall-clock work. Wandb history for the pretraining run is unchanged (naive accounting there); this only applies to the cooldown.

### Adjacent commit contents on branch `june_tpu_67b_a2b`

- [`200f995326`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/200f995326) — step-141k launcher + `resume_data_offset` extension on `GrugMoeLaunchConfig2xBS`
- [`0a2b32cd84`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0a2b32cd84) — hybrid-attn MFU accounting (`lm_flops_per_token` sliding_window params + `GrugModelConfig.hybrid_attention_flops_accounting` flag + `override_output_path` pin on the pretraining launcher to defend against the config-hash shift)

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up: two 262k context-extension probes from the same step-156000 checkpoint above.

## Runs

| variant | qk_mult | wandb | state |
|---|---|---|---|
| formula-scaled (`1.3 · (0.1·ln(32)+1)`) | 1.75 | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k) | finished |
| held from step-141k cooldown | 1.57 | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k_qk157) | running |

## Launchers

- qk=1.75: [`experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_step156k_seq262k_bs256_ctx4_muon.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/june_tpu_67b_a2b/experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_step156k_seq262k_bs256_ctx4_muon.py)
- qk=1.57: [`experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_step156k_seq262k_bs256_ctx4_muon_qk157.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/june_tpu_67b_a2b/experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_step156k_seq262k_bs256_ctx4_muon_qk157.py)

Both resume from the step-141k cooldown's `step-156000` checkpoint above.

## Design spec

- **seq_len**: 65,536 → **262,144** (4× extension).
- **BS**: 1024 → **256** sequences → tokens/step stays at 256 · 262,144 = 67.1 M (matches the step-141k cooldown's per-step token budget).
- **Steps**: 1,000 (step 156,000 → 157,000) → **67.1 B tokens** total.
- **LR**: linear decay from 5 % of source peak (0.000264, matches cooldown exit LR) → 1 % of source peak (0.0000528), no ramp. Implementation pins the resume schedule's abstract "peak" to 0.000264 with `min_lr_ratio=0.2` so the floor lands at exactly `0.000264 · 0.2 = 0.0000528`.
- **qk_mult**: 1.75 (`1.3 · (0.1·ln(32) + 1) = 1.7506`, rounded) vs. 1.57 (held from the step-141k cooldown, which used `1.3 · (0.1·ln(8) + 1) = 1.5703`). Both applied Q-only as a single logit multiplier (one-sided YaRN; note this delivers `mscale` on logits, not the paper's `mscale²`).
- **Data continuation**: exact per-token — `resume_data_offset = (13,500·8,192·8,192 + 15,000·1,024·65,536) / 262,144 = 7,296,000` samples. The launcher builds a 3-stage BS schedule `[(0, 46), (36000, 47), (156000, 256)]` that hits exactly 7,296,000 cumulative samples at step 156,000 (zero re-consumption AND zero skip). Post-run cumulative mix-2 consumption = **1.980 T tokens** (98.99% of the 2 T mix-2 design budget).
- **Checkpoints / evals**: every 250 steps (4 total: 156,250 / 156,500 / 156,750 / 157,000).
- **Mesh** on v4-2048 (1024 chips): `(replica_dcn=1, data=256, context=4, expert=1, model=1)`. `batch_shards = replica · data · expert = 256`, `per_device_parallelism = 1`. `context_axis_size = 4` shards the seq axis → `seq_per_device = 65,536` (identical chip-local seq to the step-141k cooldown, our known-good memory point).

## Context-parallel implementation

Landed on this branch as a self-contained addition; `context_axis_size = 1` is a no-op vs. the pre-CP code path.

- **Mesh axis** (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/sharding.py`): added `"context"` to `_GRUG_MESH_AXIS_NAMES`; `compact_grug_mesh` now takes `context_axis_size`. `_batch_axes()` returns the full flat-token axes and now includes `"context"` when present so MoE psums / shard_maps reduce over the correct set.
- **Grug MoE model** (`experiments/grug/moe/model.py`): seq axis on Q / residual stream / MLP / embed / output_proj sharded on `"context"` via helpers `_seq_spec_3d` / `_seq_spec_4d` / `_token_spec`. K/V explicitly resharded to seq=`None` before splash (splash's TPU entry refuses `kv_seq_shards > 1`), i.e. the **all-gather-KV** flavor of CP.
- **RoPE cache**: `_apply_half_rope` reshards its precomputed cos/sin to `P(None, "context", None, None)` so the per-shard broadcast against context-sharded Q/K lines up.
- **Segment IDs**: `Transformer.__call__` reshards q_seg to `P(_BATCH_AXES, "context")` and kv_seg to `P(_BATCH_AXES, None)` before passing the mask to splash, so splash's per-shard segment-id shape check matches.
- **Router / QB shard_map**: uses `_token_axes()` (batch + context) for the shard_map in_specs and `pmean` so the QB threshold pmean reduces across both data and context shards.
- **Splash kernel wrapping** (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py`): the splash kernel is now passed as an input to `shard_map` with its own `manual_sharding_spec` (mirroring the classical levanter path). Prior closure-capture would leave `fwd_mask_info.q_sequence` at global shape, and splash's forward broadcast would fail against the local `q_seq_len`. Each mask_info leaf is `jax.reshard`ed to the manual spec before the shard_map, since shard_map now rejects mismatched in_specs.
- **(B,S)↔(B*S) reshapes**: `_flatten_bs` / `_unflatten_bs` helpers wrap `jnp.reshape` with explicit `out_sharding` (`_token_spec()` and `_seq_spec_3d()` respectively). einops's `rearrange` goes through `array.reshape()` with no sharding hint, which JAX can't lower when two sharded axes fuse into one.
- **Trainer mesh** (`experiments/grug/moe/launch_2x_bs.py`): passes `"context": context_axis_size` into the TrainerConfig's `MeshConfig` so `data_axis_size` (used for the BS-divisibility check) reflects only the actual batch shards.
- **Loss parity** verified at `context = {1, 2, 4}` for a small config: identical loss at c=2, bf16-precision noise (~1e-6) at c=4.

## Status

- qk=1.75 finished all 1000 steps. Train loss dropped 1.325 → **1.159** across the extension; paloma macro-loss 2.177 → **2.208** (small uptick from a fresh eval at the new seq/temperature; c4_en, dolma, m2d2, redpajama all continue improving during the 1000 steps).
- qk=1.57 in flight, tracking qk=1.75 closely so far.
- Known artifact: `wikitext_103` and `ptb` paloma tags read `0.0` in both runs. Root cause: `TokenSeqDataset.async_len = total_tokens // seq_len` uses integer division, so any val cache smaller than one 262k window (wikitext_103 ~247k tokens, ptb ~86k tokens) yields **0** eval sequences. Not a training bug; only affects small paloma tags at long seq_len.

Run multiple experiments, varying the following factors:
- qk_mult. This specifies the attention 'sharpness' (how strongly can it natively pick out a single target). It started at 1.3 during 8k seqlen, then was bumped to 1.57 during 65k seqlen. This is a softer version of yarn mscale. For 262k, could hold at 1.57, or bump to ~1.75 or 2. Increasing may help on longer documents and slightly hurt on shorter documents. Previously tried an experiment bumping it only on global layers, didn't help. (However may be worth it on this 65k->262k extension)
